FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   POSSIBILITY OF MEETING WITH QUEBEC TO REDEFINE ITS OBJECTIVES WITH CONFEDERATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion.
Yesterday, the Quebec Minister of Communications stated that if this government continues to centralize everything, it could, if it remains in power a few years, bring about the split-up of Canadian federalism and Quebec separation.
Since the statement made by an official representative of the Quebec government shows a growing concern among Quebec authorities and consequently among Quebecers generally, and recognizing also the centralizing position of this government which daily threatens the objectives aimed at by the BNA Act, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey):
That the House unanimously instruct the Prime Minister to call a meeting between the Quebec government and the federal government to reassess the legitimate objectives of the Quebec government within Confederation.

speechtext:

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD RESIGNATION OF MRS. PLUMPTRE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RESTORE CREDIBILITY OF BOARD
ANTI-INFLATION BOARD RESIGNATION OF MRS. PLUMPTRE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RESTORE CREDIBILITY OF BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a question for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the co-chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board resigned on the very day that we saw almost a record increase in the consumer price index. Since one of the original reasons for her nomination as co-chairman of the board was her great credibility with Canadians, especially the consumer, may I ask the Minister of Finance what immediate action, after this serious resignation, is the government prepared to take to restore the credibility of the Anti-Inflation Board with Canadians in general and consumers in particular?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD RESIGNATION OF MRS. PLUMPTRE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RESTORE CREDIBILITY OF BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are two questions of fact: in the first place, Mrs. Plumptre was not the co-chairman, but the vice-chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board and in the second place the resignation did not occur yesterday. It occurred, I think I am correct in saying, on June 1 or some seven to ten days ago when she indicated in a letter to the Prime Minister that the six month period that had been discussed with her at the time she took on the role, had been reached and for personal reasons she proposed to stand down. With regard to her replacement, there have indeed been some considerations and discussions in this regard and we hope to be able to make an announcement at a very early date.

Mr. Speaker, virtually all of those questions were answered yesterday. The price increases were described very fully by Statistics Canada in the release issued which indicated it was the price of beef and the impact of certain provincial budgetary decisions such as the pricing of tobacco and alcohol which had an effect on the consumer price index in the month of May. With regard to the other details of pricing decisions by the Anti-Inflation Board, from time to time the board issues releases. I would be prepared to make a collection for the hon. gentleman and make certain that they get into his hands so that he can review them.
As to the question of the backlog, as I mentioned to his colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, of course the Board has not proceeded as quickly as it would have liked to in dealing with cases generally, one of the principal reasons being that a number of occasions they have paused to consider fully cases that have raised a lot of public comment, such as the Thompson case. The board has been prepared to go back and talk again to the parties rather than make a final and summary decision. The board will be trying to make its decisions as quickly and effectively as it can. I think the chairman is concerned about seeing that each party who feels he has not been fairly treated will have full opportunity to state his case before the final decision is made.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct my question to the Minister of Finance. As both labour and consumers have little confidence in the board because at present their interests are not vigorously represented within the board, would the minister, in view of the necessity of fully disclosing the operations of the board to the public, arrange the immediate referral of the administration of the board to a committee of the House, which would call witnesses and hear evidence in order to assess the board's performance and the resources it enjoys for doing its job? speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):

Mr. Speaker, I would have to correct the hon. gentleman with regard to the membership of the board. There are two labour representatives; one is Mr. Ladyman of Winnipeg, whose lifelong career has been in the labour movement; the other is Mr. Chapman, from Vancouver, whose metier as well has been in the labour area. We will be seeking appointees to the board who have Mrs. Plumptre's specific experience in the consumer area; although I would have to say that the membership of the board generally has been sensitive to consumer concerns, as evidenced by the decisions which have been made.
Finally, with regard to the proposal that the members of the board and its staff should be involved in hearings before a parliamentary committee, it seems to me that, following the line taken by several members opposite, it would be much more valuable if their time was spent dealing with the problem of inflation in Canada rather than in conducting another set of hearings.

subtopic: RESIGNATION OF MRS. PLUMPTRE-ACTION ON RECOMMENDATION FOR MONITORING SYSTEM FOR MARKETING BOARDS

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: RESIGNATION OF MRS. PLUMPTRE-ACTION ON RECOMMENDATION FOR MONITORING SYSTEM FOR MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Since it now appears obvious to everybody but the minister that Mrs. Plumptre's timing exemplifies in a very dramatic way her frustration over her inability to get this government to act on the prices issue, will the minister advise what action the Anti-Inflation Board and the government are taking on one of the recommendations made by Mrs. Plumptre with respect to a monitoring system of marketing boards in Canada and some agreement with the provinces in this regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: RESIGNATION OF MRS. PLUMPTRE-ACTION ON RECOMMENDATION FOR MONITORING SYSTEM FOR MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having been the person who first spoke to Mrs. Plumptre about taking on this assignment, I feel I must at least dispel the suggestion put in the first part of the question. When I first approached Mrs. Plumptre in October, her first answer was negative. I would rather not put these matters before the House because they are of a confidential nature. But in face of two opposition parties which really are fabricating a whole series of interpretations which are completely opposed to the truth, I feel I must say that at first Mrs. Plumptre refused, because of family and personal reasons, to accept the assignment. Finally, she took it on but made it quite clear she would resign within a period of a few months-that she was only taking the job to help in the transition. Wait to hear the results of the press confer-

ence, Mr. Speaker, but I am stating the facts as they happened. She made it clear at the outset that she would resign in a few months. If her resignation now comes as a surprise to the opposition, it certainly has not come as a surprise to the government. The timing, if anything, was favourable to the government because Mrs. Plumptre stayed on longer than she said at first she would. Her letter of resignation was dated June 1, before the figures of the last consumer price index were known, and I therefore repeat that this whole line of questioning, if not malicious, is extremely ignorant.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR TABLING OF FEDERAL POSITION PAPERS

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR TABLING OF FEDERAL POSITION PAPERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question, of which I have given notice, is directed to the Prime Minister and relates to the crucial Conference of First Ministers which is to begin on Monday. I know that members of the press are to be briefed on Monday morning with respect to the federal position papers, prior to the next sitting of the House. Will the Prime Minister undertake to table these papers today so that Members of Parliament may have an opportunity to study the federal position?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR TABLING OF FEDERAL POSITION PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is our intention to table the federal position papers on Monday at two o'clock. The custom, a long established one, has been that position papers of either the provincial or federal governments for federal-provincial conferences should not be released in advance, and would not be released in advance unless there were agreement from the parties that that could and should be done. Obviously, the federal government acting alone would have no objection to tabling this paper now, but I feel that this would be somewhat of a breach of faith with the custom established with the provinces.
In fact, my office has received representations from at least four provinces following a partial leak which I understand occurred a few days ago, from we do not know what source. These representations are to the effect that we should not release these position papers. The premiers wanted to be in a position on Monday to react to them and not be forced to react to them before that time because of the release of the federal position papers. This has been the custom in the past.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR TABLING OF FEDERAL POSITION PAPERS

see what great advantage the opposition would get from having them at four rather than on Monday. What was leaked to the press-and I have not seen it-certainly could not be the final document, which was worked on until very recently. I would certainly agree at that stage to give copies to the hon. lady and to any other members of the opposition who would want to take cognizance of it before the document was actually tabled in Parliament at two, presuming that the House would not object to our releasing it to some members before it was tabled in the House as a whole.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
That this House questions the application of the Department of Transport's "user pay" concept as it applies to "mature and immature" regions of Canada and to different modes of transportation, and urges the minister to clarify the guidelines for implementation of the policy and to explain any alterations contemplated in it.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this motion I really welcome the opportunity to discuss one of the main obligations of the government, such as governing the country of Canada. Transportation has historically played a very important role in the development of this country. In the last two or three years this government indicated to us that it was going to do something about transportation. Over and over again the government stated that it had a concept which would greatly assist Canada in its development, namely rationalization of our transportation policy. Some years ago, a former minister of transport said that the transportation policy of Canada was in a mess. We all agreed with him, acknowledged his frankness in admitting that, praised him for admitting it and hoped that he would come up with a solution. During the election campaign in June, 1974, the Liberal party pranced across the country suggesting that it had some solutions, and the Prime Min-

June 11, 1976

ister (Mr. Trudeau) said they were not idle election promises but they were promises to do something about Canada's transportation problems.
In the Speech from the Throne in 1974, the government indicated its desire to see transportation used as an instrument of policy designed to achieve broad national, social and economic objectives. Well, we are still wondering. In fact, on the question of transportation policy today we could ask where we are going. In western Canada, the Stavely commission is studying the cost of moving grain. Also, in western Canada the Hall commission is studying the question of rail line abandonment and the rationalization of trackage. The CTC is travelling across the country hearing briefs with regard to passenger traffic. We wonder where all this is leading us.
As late as June, 1975, the government announced a new transportation policy. The government and the then minister said the principal advice on transportation policy would be in the hands of the government and they were really going to take over much of the role played by the CTC until that time. Now we are in June, 1976, and what have we seen this government actually do? We have a new Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). He has bought the line handed down by, I suppose, the civil service which said that we must work on a "user pay" concept. I have always felt that transportation could serve the people of Canada a great deal better if users had a little more say before they were asked to pay.
Members of the transport committee travelled to Vancouver. One of the things they learned was that the federal government's policy had held back the development of that port. Nearly everybody concerned with the question of transportation into and around Vancouver harbour seemed to admit that. The committee then travelled down to Seattle and saw Canadian produce moving in and out of that port both to and from Canada when much of the goods should have been coming in through Vancouver. Our port facilities and transportation policy on the movement of goods into the port from the centre of the country and the prairies have not kept pace with the need which has been demonstrated in our trading policy with the Pacific rim countries.
What are this government and the Minister of Transport going to do about it? There are numerous commissions studying conditions, of course. We have a country concerned with transportation and productivity, because transportation plays a great part in our economy. It can keep inflation down and increase productivity, or increase costs; so it is important to know which direction the minister is taking. The only conclusion I can come to is that the minister seems bent on increasing freight rates, increasing the cost of air passenger travel, increasing the cost of rail passenger travel and, recently, increasing the cost of shipping.
An article in this morning's Globe and Mail reported that Nova Scotia was complaining about this government's actions in regard to Bill C-61 which will increase the cost of shipping in Canada. Shipping costs went up on the Great Lakes last year, and we have seen rail costs and freight costs go up. All this makes it more difficult for our
Transportation Policy
produce to get to world markets because of a poor and ailing transportation system. We want to know what the government is going to do about it. How are they going to apply the "user pay" concept?
In June, 1975, a policy was announced which spoke of "mature and immature" areas. What does that mean? What are "immature" areas? At various times in committee the minister stated that subsidies would have to paid in immature areas, but in areas where competition had matured, competition would take care of the cost and no subsidy would be necessary. The government did away with some of the subsidies for the maritimes with regard to the movement of freight, so I suppose they consider it a mature area. I am sure it is not considered that way by many of the people living in the maritimes and attempting to do business there. This government has failed to clearly enunciate what they mean by "user pay" and what they mean by "mature and immature" areas. I hope the minister takes the opportunity to explain to the House and to the country what he means by the use of those terms in the national transportation policy.
It is not good enough for the government to suggest that they are going to do something about rail passenger service, or to think that giving $30 million to the CPR is going to bring about any great improvement. We know that 3.4 million people travel in what is commonly referred to as the Quebec-Windsor corridor. In 1974 the government had a grandiose scheme to set up a transportation authority for passenger traffic, something like Amtrak in the United States. But they have not done it. Instead, they proclaimed loudly that the $167 million subsidy for rail passenger traffic was too high.
They say they are going to adopt the "user pay" concept and that people who use a certain mode of transportation will have to pay for it. They do not mention that the government operates something like 86 airports and loses $243 million in maintaining them. Some time ago the minister suggested that under the "user pay" concept landing fees would have to be increased. If fees were increased for all the smaller planes using airports, that would in no way pay for the cost of maintaining those airports.
When he announced the new transportation policy, the minister also stated that the government was going to increase competition with Air Canada. In November, 1975, I asked him if this meant that the 25 per cent formula that controls CP Air would be done away with. Earlier this spring I asked the same question in the transport committee, and the minister replied that they were trying to find a way of removing the 25 per cent formula and allowing CP Air to grow. But we still have no clearcut explanation of how this will come about.
In 1965 we had a regional air policy that was designed to promote the growth of clearly established regional airlines. We have five regional airlines in Canada and have built up a huge number of primary air carriers, sometimes referred to as third-level carriers, but as yet the government has not announced any policy with regard to them. All this uncertainty with regard to freight rates, air passenger traffic and costs is cause for a great deal of apprehension to the users of our modes of transportation. Is the "user pay" concept going to apply fairly to all modes of transportation?

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
When the new transportation policy was announced in June, 1975, the Department of Transport stated that buses were the only mode of transportation not subsidized. One could argue that buses receive a tremendous subsidy through the maintenance of our highways. In fact, figures released recently suggest that all users of highways only pay for about 67 per cent of the cost of maintaining them. Buses make good use of the highways and they perform efficiently. In the "user pay" concept, will the government step in and ensure it is applied fairly to bus, rail and air traffic?
Ottawa has been the centre of a very recent experiment in the movement of passengers, Mr. Speaker. The government set up an experimental STOL service between Ottawa and Montreal which lost a great deal of money. Although the service is discontinued, we do not know if the government intends to reintroduce it. We have not been told. This leads to uncertainty.
The government wants to set up a new kind of rail passenger service between Ottawa and Montreal, Montreal and Windsor, and Montreal and Toronto, but has not specified clearly what it intends to do. We are entering an era of high energy costs, but the government has not spelled out clearly which mode of travel it prefers or how that mode will be developed or even financed. We do not know the government's direction. If we bound into one volume all the press releases the Department of Transport has put out in the past ten years, we would have an encyclopaedia of the government's good intentions. But the government has done few of the things set out in glowing terms in those news releases.
The minister said quite clearly that Air Canada may lose some of its shorter routes. Apparently, regional airlines, including CP Air, will be allowed to bid on some shorter routes. If it is found that regional carriers need less subsidy to operate such routes, Air Canada will lose them. To me, that will be a step in the wrong direction. As it is, too many airlines are operating in the United States. There has been some attempt to trim the fat off airline operations in that country. Here, in Canada, the government's move may encourage the proliferation of airlines. Instead of dealing with one airline in trouble, some day we may have to deal with six or seven all in trouble.
What is the government's policy on freight movement? The Minister of Transport has created much apprehension on the prairies and in western Canada generally. Many people in western Canada suspect him of being in bed with the CPR and of being in favour of getting rid of the Crowsnest pass rates. Some time ago he said in Edmonton that the Crowsnest pass rates had to go; it was only a matter of time.

speechtext:
I do not mind seeing Liberal members clap their hands when it is suggested that the minister suggested the Crowsnest pass rates have to go. At least that clears the air. We on the prairies, particularly those in the minister's province, want to know the Liberal party's intentions with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. If we know the government's position, the uncertainty will disappear.
In 1974 the government convened the western economic opportunities conference in Calgary. Western Canadian representatives presented their ideas concerning railway tracks. The government has not acted. We have seen no answers and few results. The government said it would devise a system for grouping commodities with a view to bringing about more favourable freight rates. There was much talk, but that is all. So far as we know the conference brought few results and answered few western Canadian complaints about the movement of goods.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The government does not care.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
The minister has said in the past that freight rates governing the movement of goods west should not be greater than those governing the movement of goods from central Canada to Vancouver. But this policy has not been implemented. It still costs more to ship from Hamilton to Calgary than from Hamilton to Vancouver. We have heard much talk but we have seen little action in this regard.
Some time ago the Canadian Transport Commission studied the movement of rapeseed, but its findings were not released. The minister said he would make a decision on the matter. He did, but that decision is not clear. He said certain discrepancies must be eliminated and the rate gap narrowed. But he wanted to move up the bottom rates rather than bring down the top. That did not suit the people of western Canada, who still wonder what the minister's policy is with regard to freight movement. In North America the natural flow of traffic has been from north to south, and vice versa, rather than from east to west. Perhaps that accounts for some of our difficulties.
As we see it, transportation in this country must play a vital role in making our economy sound-and developing the various regions of Canada economically so that, in competition with one another, they will be able to grow and better serve central Canadian-indeed, all Canadian consumer markets. As we see it, also, this government's policies have created much apprehension and solved few of our difficulties. Supposedly, it enunciated a new policy one year ago. It talks a great deal about the concept of users paying for service. I say that users should have more say in these matters.
It talks of certain mature and immature regions, but does not define what those terms mean. At present, shippers and manufacturers do not always know if they are entitled to a subsidy. In this country we have traditional subsidies coming under the Maritime Freight Rates Act in the maritimes and the Crowsnest pass rates in western Canada. But the minister has already said that the Crowsnest pass rates in western Canada are to be reviewed. That
June 11, 1976

has created much apprehension. I suggest that the minister should explain in greater detail exactly what he intends.
Two years ago the government talked of introducing a new transportation act, because the original act passed in 1967 can no longer serve Canada adequately. We are still awaiting that new transportation act, which I suppose would incorporate policies the government announced over one year ago. Perhaps if this session continues another year the government may introduce the bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to put before the House some answers to questions asked throughout the country concerning the transportation policy of the government as now being developed. Transportation in Canada is most important. For that reason, what we do in transportation is most important as well. Because transportation is costly, it is a large item affecting the over-all cost of living of Canadians. Therefore, if we manage our transport system badly we shall lose a great deal of money.
I want to talk today particularly about the cost of transportation and where our policy with regard thereto has taken us so far. When my predecessor, the now Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand), said several years ago that transportation in this country was a mess, he did not mean that people involved in transportation in Canada were doing their job badly. He did not mean that about the people involved in the various modes of transportation. He did not even mean that about the people inside government departments who work on various aspects of transportation policy and issues. What he meant to say was that the policy was a mess, that the conglomeration of approaches to transportation in Canada which had developed over the years was full of inconsistencies and contradictions, that it had built into Canada tremendous costs in the way of non-productive expenditure that was in fact counterproductive.
He pointed the finger, in the bold way he has, directly at government as having the responsibility, at least today, to put the situation right, even though, clearly, the problem he was speaking about was the conglomeration of problems of governments year after year and over many decades in Canada. In his bold way, as well, my predecessor began the work of putting right the mess in transportation. Last summer he put before the House and the people of Canada the broad outline of the analysis of our transportation difficulties and the broad direction in which we ought to go in order to find solutions. I want to make it very clear that in pursuing this work I feel a complete consonance, a complete "in-tuneness" with my predecessor in the work he has done. I express my gratitude to him for the way in which he began it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I have been saying all across this country that we have to be realistic about our transportation costs. This has been translated into the expression that the user pay. I want to put that expression clearly before the House in the proper context. The proper context is that transportation costs are real and someone must pay them. Those who do not think the user should pay have to appreciate that they
Transportation Policy
are pointing the finger and saying that someone else should pay. If you do not like the expression "user pay", you have to defend the proposition that the non-user ought to pay for transportation costs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That term "non-user" can, of course, be put in other ways. He can be called the taxpayer. It can be the taxpayer who is supposed to pay part of the cost. However, those politicians who like to make it appear that by fighting "user pay" they are fighting against and eliminating high costs to the great advantage of the country, are deluding themselves and the country. It leads to the continuance of the very kind of patchwork policies, suitable to particular political demands, which created the mess in the first place.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Those patchwork policies were frequently devised, and subsidies piled one on top of another, in answer to particular political demands which by themselves were popular in meeting a particular cause of a particular individual. It did not change the cost to the country. It had the impact over the years of unnecessarily increasing the total cost to the taxpayer, building a transportation system more costly than it otherwise would have been. It is to put this right that we are now launched upon the reform of transportation policy.
I want hon. members, particularly on this side of the House, to appreciate that this exercise will not be easy. These particular band-aids went on as political offerings to meet a particular demand for a particular area. There is a good deal of attachment to those band-aids and a good deal of fear about the pain that will be involved, as it will, every time you remove a band-aid.
We will only be able to succeed in improving our transportation policy in Canada, and thereby our transportation system with our dollars, if we are prepared to be strong enough to stand up politically and draw the picture of what we are trying to accomplish in terms of removing the band-aids, not individually but one by one, in order to remove them in total so that the body politic of transportation in the end can be healthier as a result of removing the band-aids rather than covering them over with more political band-aids.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I want to make it clear that there are very good reasons in this country for direct policy action to accomplish particular ends. Direct policy action to improve regional development is clearly an objective that this government asserts. Redistribution of wealth is another objective which this government asserts. However, generally speaking we will be better off if we try to accomplish those objectives directly instead of hiding an apparent accomplishment of those objectives behind a transportation distortion and subsidy program. That is the point I am trying to make.
The point is that these distortions in transportation costs in fact lead to distortions in production and a higher total cost in Canada. For example, it may be effective to the

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
producer of grain on the prairies to have a low freight rate. There is, simultaneously, a more normal cost-reflecting rate on meat which might be produced from that grain. That is a serious disadvantage to the prairie region, in terms of the encouragement of the shipment to Japan and Italy of grain instead of the shipment to those markets and the creation in those markets of a demand for our beef, pork and similar products. The substitution of meat for grain might create jobs in processing and development, the very things that the prairie region wants. Does it, therefore, prefer the shipment of grain because the cost to the shipper is lower by shipping it in that form than shipping it as beef? The important point here is that the cost to the country is significantly greater to move eight pounds of barley from the middle of Saskatchewan to Vancouver than it is to move one pound of beef. The rates may be lower, but the cost to the country is higher. Therefore, there may be an inducement to that kind of movement. Indeed, if they are much lower than the real cost reflected rate, they tend to that artificial result.
Not only do we defeat our broad purpose of being productive by producing where it is best, ideally, by economics to produce, especially when that is an area where we want to develop population, jobs and secondary industry in processing, but we end up spending more money on transportation than we would have to spend if we went about the system correctly and in a balanced way.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: You have not created any markets for beef.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The hon. member says we have not created markets for beef. We have not. That is because of this very kind of disincentive which has stood in the way of real encouragement to production.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I wish to make another very complicated point as clear as I can. I am referring to the value of the Crowsnest pass rates which I have been, obviously, discussing with regard to the low rates on grain. I want to say something about that and some very special arrangements in this country, such as the arrangement entered into with Newfoundland at the time it joined confederation when a particular and special treatment was accorded that province with regard to the movement of goods between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. That may indeed, in that sense, be rather sacred. The sacredness of the constitutional agreement with Newfoundland obviously stands. The sacredness of the tradition with regard to the Crowsnest pass is well known. But the point I am making-and I have made it in the west-is that if we have to do these things in accordance with our obligation to a region, it should be open to us to consider whether we can do them more directly rather than indirectly in the area of transportation. I have, therefore, said with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates that if this benefit were conferred more directly, and if we did not pin it on the rates, we would not only benefit the region as much in terms of dollars, but a lower-cost over-all transportation system would be brought about because we would be shipping the goods which it makes more sense to ship, instead of goods which

are shipped because of the artificially lower rate upon those goods.
In the west this is understood-only they refer to other matters. They say the low rates on ores and the higher rates on finished products are disincentives to the refining of those products in the west. Obviously, that is true, and it is exactly the kind of case I am making. It is exactly the approach which leads us to say that by and large in this country, we would be better off if the rate to which a person is exposed when facing a business decision is as close as possible to real cost. He then has to take into consideration the real cost of moving the product he wishes to move.
I do not see the advantage of taking coal out of our ground and shipping it at a certain cost to the shipper when, if we weighed all the costs to the country, including the real cost of the freight which is not being charged, it might not be a benefit to move that coal into some other market, or abroad. Why should we move it if the costs, when taken into account, are not adequately met by the gains we get from the product which is moved?

speechtext:
That is the realism I ask to be brought to the transportation system. When we talk about bringing this approach to mature transportation systems, we are, of course, talking about transportation systems in which the loading factor, the use of the system, is sufficient to make an approach which balances costs an appropriate one. I say this because I will always accept the need on occasion to take a transportation system into a remote area or to go in well in advance, for national purposes, of development which will eventually sustain that transportation system, or to connect remote areas so as to provide for the movement of people by some mode to the more settled centres of the country. When only a few people are there, it may not be possible to charge enough to meet the total cost. What we really mean when we say the user should pay is that there should be a logical cost transportation system, a low-cost transportation system, and this will most likely result if the user knows the real cost and makes his decisions accordingly.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) says that if there is "user pay", there should be "user say". To that, I say "bravo". Increasingly as we move toward the implementation of costs which are real and reflect the investment required, more and more of the people involved in the marketing of that service will have a say in the kind of service provided. I have told the airlines, for example, that I welcome input from their customers on the question of the style of facilities which are legitimate in our airports from a marketing point of view.
In the passenger area one finds one of the best examples of the problems which arise when we are prepared to distort the real cost. The papers published in connection with the 1975 study of our transportation system have been before the House and the people for a very long time, essentially unchallenged by those who have read them. It is true they have been challenged by some who have not
June 11, 1976

read them. Some of those figures are out of date now, but in my view they are still instructive.
Based on those studies, it is said that the person who travels by bus essentially pays his own way. The analysis even concluded that a fair share of the total road cost was defrayed through the gas taxes and licensing system to which buses are subject. The automobile was seen as receiving a subsidy equivalent to half a cent per passenger mile. The air passenger was seen as receiving a subsidy equal to 2 cents per passenger mile. In the case of the railroads it is higher, at 6 cents per passenger mile.
I ask hon. members: What kind of particular public purpose is there which would lead us to say that a person who travels by bus should first of all pay his own way and then, through sharing in the tax system, pay part of the costs of those who travel by car or by airplane? I ask what justification there is for that. I ask whether it is not better, if we have income distribution in mind, to face this situation straightforwardly. I do not think we would then end up taxing the bus rider to pay for the airplane traveller. If we have something else in mind, I would like to know what it is. I can see no justification for it.

Mr. Speaker, the Atl-East rate is another example of an occasion on which we embarked upon an artificiality. I say again: unless one is really embracing a principle of using a teaspoon to dig ditches by way of maintaining employment in this country, we ought not to preserve systems which lead to absurdities in terms of total cost.
The Wheat Board told us yesterday in committee that even at the Atl-East rates it costs seven cents a bushel more to move grain from the prairies to Halifax and Saint John than if it were moved by the water mode. That seven cents was worth their while to pay in order to have grain in position over the winter months for delivery when the lake and seaway system was closed. Of course, the cost to the country was much greater. This led to the result that we took grain from a farm by truck, put it in an elevator, then it was taken out again and put on a train to Thunder Bay, unloaded there, put in an elevator, cleaned, loaded into a vessel, taken to a port along the bay or lake, unloaded there, put into a terminal, then in due course loaded on a train, taken to Halifax or Saint John, and then unloaded into the final terminal.
Because of the subsidy, no one in that period of time had any incentive to look at a reasonable alternative, such as taking it from an elevator which can clean grain on the prairies, putting it on a train and taking it by unit train movement direct to Halifax, Saint John or Montreal, which can be done at very little more cost than by the water route, if all the truth be known-if we can get the truth, in terms of a real rate, from the railways, and we are trying to do that exactly these days. Those costs, unnecessary for that purpose, were thrown away. The examples go on and on, Mr. Speaker. That is the theme that we would want to develop as we examine all aspects of our transportation system.
I must say this to the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan), that when we are looking at the seaway, rail and a road running side by side, it makes no sense at all to be paying a specific subsidy or part payment of the cost if the grain go by water, making a different payment if it goes by rail, or some other payment if it goes by road. There is no justification for that at all. All that does is distort economics and it leads in the end to the construction of more facilities that are subsidized, even though that may be the more costly way of moving the product. This is what we are going to try to put right.
I want to say a few words, since the hon. member for Crowfoot did, about a couple of other issues rather than this broad, philosophic one. For instance, we are moving forward with our passenger rail examination in Canada, and we intend, as we have said, to put under one management and operation passenger rail service in this country so that it can be marketed effectively and run in a cohesive way to make maximum use of joint facilities and the interchange of track wherever it makes sense to do so. This is our firm intention. We have asked the companies to

move in that direction and we are prepared to take whatever action is needed to make sure that this result is accomplished.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting at this stage that we can necessarily approach cost recovery in all our passenger service routes which are retained, but that is consistent with what I have just said. Our problem is that we start with a transportation system that was built on certain patchwork principles, and therefore there is a certain amount of preference for some modes over others. In particular, we have without any doubt favoured, in terms of subsidy, the automobile mode over other public modes of transportation.
I am prepared to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in this country there is a real chance that passenger service can be made more attractive, that with new equipment and upgrading of lines it can be made attractive to passengers. The only way we are going to demonstrate this is by having faith in this thesis, going out and building the system and proving that it can work. We therefore propose to maintain some rail passenger services where it will not be obvious that it will be possible in the early phases to accomplish full cost recovery. We believe, of course, that we ought to discontinue those services where perhaps lack of demand is so great that the losses will be inordinate, and where alternative modes of transportation, such as a bus running alongside an unused rail passenger service, is available to the people. In those cases we ought not to spend the money; we ought, indeed, try to save it.
We also propose to continue to attempt to support public transportation in the cities of this country. When we implement the commuter policy of making some money available for commuter services, we recognize that we will only be doing part of the job that we have to do for urban transportation. We believe that it is right at this stage to support urban transportation with federal capital assistance, for much the same reason as I have described in relation to rail service. These have been in large part underused and undersupported because of the quite unnecessary and unjustified subsidies, although politically band-aid subsidies, which have been given by governments all over this country in support of the automobile, particular in regard to urban transportation.
That is a patchwork problem that has been created in large part by governments other than ours. Nevertheless, I believe we will have to try to take the lead in trying to get a change, a revolution in thinking, in favour of public transportation and away from the subsidized automobile which is so common in our cities.
It happens, of course, that both in the case of rail across the country and in the case of urban transportation system within our cities these may be modes that look particularly to the future, as we face a Canada that is becoming more and more concerned about pollution of the atmosphere, noise, and the cost of energy. Therefore, we may want in many different ways to encourage the use of these systems and certainly to avoid the use of the costly systems employed in each of these modes.
I have, Mr. Speaker, touched on some of the issues with which we will be dealing. We have, indeed, laid before the

House and the country the blueprint of a philosophy that we will be adopting, and we will continue to do this. This helps individuals to know where they may be going and to calculate what the costs to them may be in the future of various options for a transportation system. What I should like from most users, therefore, is the general conclusion on their part that if they make a mistake in examining a future course of action, looking at rates on an artificial basis instead of costs that are real, they will be looking at the wrong thing.
As far as this government is concerned, productivity in this country will be improved by this rational approach to transportation and the lowest cost alternatives being selected. Productivity will also be improved as users of transportation, both businessmen and entrepreneurs looking at business possibilities, face the real cost to this country of what they are trying to do and of what is being done, and not at artificial rates based on some band-aid, political opportunity subsidy. Those subsidies we will want to remove, and that will be our task.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) used an analogy and likened the transportation system of our country to a band-aid policy or band-aid program. He said that now he is taking these bold steps in removing the band-aids, it is going to hurt. I am glad he used that analogy because I always think of a band-aid in terms of it being used to cover a sore or a wound, the purpose of which, of course, is to protect that wound or sore from infection and to allow whatever it is you are covering to heal. The premature removal of a band-aid would, in fact, result in further harm, especially if you have not done anything to heal the wound or sore.
In fact, that is what we have here in terms of transportation in Canada. We have the minister removing these band-aids without having put anything in their place to correct the problem. Indeed, the very things he is doing- and we have analysed what he is doing in respect of giving the CPR $30 million for railway passenger services between Quebec City and Montreal-constitute another band-aid program; he is starting a new brand of band-aid program.
We in this party have always held the view that at the beginning of Canada, transportation was used as a binder; it was used to bind this country together, bringing its peoples closer. The railway system was specifically built for that purpose. It was to repel what was feared to be an American invasion from the south, and really to connect the country from coast to coast. Of course, with the improvement in telecommunications, that original purpose has been lost. There is a new role we in this party have always felt, and still feel, that transportation ought to be
June 11, 1976

playing. We feel it ought to be used as a tool by the government to eliminate regional disparity. In other words, it ought not to be considered in terms of profit for the railway companies or in terms of the phrase "let the user pay" which the minister uses so often, but, rather, to eliminate regional disparity.
I congratulate the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) for having chosen this particular motion to put before the House, giving us an opportunity to debate it. A few years ago the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Mar-chand) who was minister of transport at the time, had some interesting ideas about transportation. We heard that transportation in this country should serve the country, and that our transportation policy should be used in conjunction with other policies to improve the lives of Canadians. Specifically, the minister said:
What we are proposing states that the transportation system should be accessible, equitable and efficient, rather than economic, efficient and adequate. The notion of efficiency is not lost, but the emphasis is on service to Canadians.
That is a far cry from what we hear today. Today we hear the Minister of Transport trying to throw the country back 100 years with his concept of "let the user pay." Mind you, this "let the user pay" concept is pretty selective. It is pretty clear that some users will be paying a much higher percentage of the cost than others. It is also clear that some parts of this country are going to pay a lot more for transportation than others. I am not just talking about the dollar cost of taking a train, nor am I talking just about the dollar cost of shipping material from one place to another; I am talking about the cost of unemployment in parts of Canada, both in social and economic terms, and the destruction of the potential for job-producing secondary industry.
If this government was really concerned about these problems, it would present this House with a comprehensive transportation policy. The government would present us with a policy which we could debate, analyse and legislate on. It would show the people of Canada exactly how parliament intended to use transportation over the coming years and what could be expected across this country because of it. Instead, the government is surreptitiously making changes in a "half-fast" way which masquerades as a transportation policy.
For example, the government announces a cutback in transcontinental rail service by sending the matter to a committee of the Canadian Transport Commission, giving the committee instructions that can only result in the choice of alternative cutbacks. For example, this government chooses to change freight rate arrangements at a time when commissions are already studying the subject. While this goes on, low-income Canadians and the poor regions of Canada continue to suffer from policies aimed at keeping them in their place.
In northern Ontario particularly, where I come from, freight rates for years have played a major role in preventing the growth of secondary industry. Relative to Ontario as a whole, northern Ontario suffers from stagnant population growth, a lack of growth in employment, a high rate of emigration and low levels of per capita income. As a result of that emigration, northern Ontario will lose one federal seat in this House, dropping from 12 to 11.
Transportation Policy
The fact is that the economics of transportation are such that they tend to favour the transportation of materials in their unprocessed state to their final destination. This has pretty obvious implications for areas based on the production of prime products, such as northern Ontario. We do not have a great deal of information on this subject, for the very reason the minister gave in the House earlier today: he said the railway companies have never provided us with their freight rate structures and the costing of their rates.
Why can the government not act on behalf of Canadians and demand from the railway companies their freight rate structures? This is a veritable jungle, and if the government cannot get that information from the railway companies, how can it plan any kind of program? How can it put into place any kind of transportation policy, when it does not have the facts? It seems to me the government should obtain these facts before it takes all the little band-aids off all the little sores across the country.
Over the years we have gained some information. Here are some examples I was able to get my hands on in 1974. These examples amply illustrate the discriminatory manner in which present freight rate structures discriminate against northern Ontario and areas like ours. It costs about $9 to ship a ton of iron ore pellets from Copper Cliff, which is in my riding, to Pittsburgh, a distance of 800 miles. But it costs about $90 to ship a ton of fertilizer, a manufactured product, from Toronto to Sudbury, a distance of 242 miles. A 500-pound shipment from Kirkland Lake to Toronto costs $95.20 a ton for a distance of 398 miles. The same sized shipment from Winnipeg to Udora, Saskatchewan, a distance of 394 miles, would cost only $55.20 a ton. Using another example, shipments of plywood from Hearst, northern Ontario, to Eugene, Oregon, cost $74.80 a ton. But similar plywood can be shipped by rail from Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, to Eugene, Oregon, for only $60 a ton-despite the fact that Dartmouth is 1,000 miles farther from Eugene than Hearst is.
Here is another example. A shipment of forest products from Kapuskasing to Green Bay, Wisconsin, must travel a circuitous route via Detroit, travelling a total distance of 1,449 miles. A shorter route via Sault Ste. Marie to Michigan would mean a journey of only 625 miles, but the railways will not authorize this. It is pretty clear from information like this that those rates and routes unreasonably discourage the growth of primary and secondary industry in the north. This is discrimination which the present national transportation policy is supposed to eliminate. Yet the discrimination exists because this government will not institute a rational transportation policy for this country based on service to our citizens rather than based on corporate benefits.
If anyone doubts the effect this has on the north, all one has to do is to study the latest census data comparing northern Ontario with Ontario as a whole. In Ontario 22.3 per cent of the work force is involved in managerial, administrative and clerical work. In the north, the figure is
15.1	per cent. But a better example is in the area of machining, product fabricating, assembling and repairing:
12.1	per cent of the Ontario work force is involved in those jobs, but for northern Ontario the figure is only 8.3 per cent.

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
In Sudbury, for example, when the world price for nickel is buoyant and the two levels of governement, federal and provincial, are threatened into bribing INCO and Falcon-bridge to produce there rather than at their branch plants abroad, there is a boom in employment in the north. But in the bust, when the lay-offs come, my area faces severe unemployment. When this happens, the community begins to disintegrate as families drift away to other locations in search of work. The economic base of the community fails as taxes decline and the community as a whole suffers. And do not think the companies do not know the power they hold in that part of Ontario.
Secondary industry in the north would break the strangle-hold of those companies by providing alternative employment and by broadening the economic base of the community, thus minimizing adverse effects in any slowdown in the resource sector for whatever reason. But this situation is not peculiar to northern Ontario alone. The people of western Canada have for years experienced development problems directly related to the lack of any national and comprehensive transportation system. The people of western Canada have traditionally opposed the railway monopolies which sought to make enormous profits off their backs, and over the years they have won some fights. The result of one of these fights was the creation of the Crowsnest rate arrangement which guaranteed fair prices for the shipping of their products.
It was MP Reynold Rapp who in the early sixties introduced a bill in this House whereby rapeseed would be included under those rate arrangements. This allowed rapeseed to be delivered in the east or the west at the lowest possible rates. These rate arrangements meant that western farmers could move their grain to market at reasonable costs, and in return the railway companies got other considerations.
But now the minister wants to give the companies more than the healthy profits they already enjoy on freight. In fact, commissions have been set up to study this whole problem. But the transport ministry has prejudged the outcome of the Hall commission and the Snavely commission, presently examining this problem, by his recent actions on rapeseed products freight rates and his proposal for increased seaway tolls. The Minister of Transport talks about consultation, but it appears he has already made up his mind without consulting the provinces. The order in council of April 13 removing rapeseed oil and meal was made only five days after mailing the latest cost information to the provinces, which they view to be inadequate and inaccurate.
The federal government is reneging on its promise at the western economic opportunities conference in 1973 to support further processing of raw materials in the west. Compensatory rates for movement of rapeseed products places the total western rapeseed crushing and processing industry in jeopardy. It will increase the anomaly in favour of crushing rapeseed in eastern Canada over crushing it in western Canada.
The minister's "the user shall pay" policy will wipe out any hope of transportation being used to achieve broad national, social and economic goals. People will be discriminated against because of where they live. The freight

rate structure which discourages processing in western Canada will only worsen regional disparities.
According to successive Liberal and Tory governments, westerners are not supposed to be able to process their own products in western Canada. They are supposed to grow the raw product and send it to central Canada for manufacturing, then buy it back. This latest freight rate controversy on rapeseed products has caused a great deal of disappointment among western Canadians. It is quite clear that the federal government has abandoned its promise to eliminate the freight rate discrimination on processed western products in favour of having the processing done in eastern Canada. The further suggestion to solve this problem by increasing the freight rate on unprocessed rapeseed is another attack on the Crowsnest rates before the results of the Hall and Snavely commissions are completed. The work of these commissions and of the people who appeared at formal hearings is being ignored by the rhinister who has already made up his mind.
The minister has been playing around for two years with feed grains on the open market. The producers have shown a distinct preference for dealing through the Canadian Wheat Board rather than the open market. Now the Wheat Board will be required to offer feed grains at prices competitive with those of U.S. corn. Reducing the feed freight assistance will mean lower feed grain prices to western producers. This feed grains policy will also put the western livestock producer at a disadvantage with respect to the eastern livestock producer. In western Canada, as in northern Ontario, Canadians are being treated as hewers of wood and drawers of water. The Minister of Transport is perpetuating and intensifying this problem through policies which discriminate against the establishment of secondary industry in the prairies and northern Ontario. Recent attempts to raise costs for the use of the St. Lawrence Seaway is another example of a change in our transportation policy that will cost our western farmers plenty, without any thought for the social and economic costs beyond the crass concept of "let the user pay".
Now let us turn to Atlantic Canada. The Atlantic provinces are in the same boat as the west and northern Ontario. The specific example I have chosen to exemplify the transportation mess in Atlantic Canada is Bill C-61. The theory behind Bill C-61 is that it will give Canadian shipping a boost, and to a lesser extent the Canadian shipbuilding industry. The bill makes it mandatory that ships sailing from one Canadian port to another Canadian port must be of Canadian registry.
Canadian shippers and the SIU strongly agree with this bill, for their own reasons. The SIU is hoping for expanded membership, and the Canadian shippers, a relative handful of companies, would have no foreign competitors. There is an exemption clause in Bill C-61 which is very germane to this particular transportation problem, and which will allow firms to ship with foreign flags if there are no Canadian vessels available. This clause is vague and subjective. The government could veto shipping contracts if a Canadian shipper offered a vessel, no matter what the cost difference. Companies are not going to expose themselves to such a hazardous proposition. Already one firm has claimed that it will not build in Cape Breton because of the
June 11, 1976

proposed changes. This was in regard to iron ore. It will be cheaper to send the iron ore to Rotterdam, in Europe, than from Ungava to Cape Breton for processing.
Canadian shippers, perhaps in anticipation of the bill, have drastically raised their fees, forcing marginally profitable firms like SYSCO to switch to commonwealth ships. If this measure passes, the maritimes will be at the mercy of these shippers. For this law to work, this government must build a Crown-owned merchant marine, but unfortunately the government makes no such guarantee. Hence, we may inherit the worst of both worlds.
Presently, shipping rates are having the effect of keeping down rail and trucking rates in coastal areas, because if there is a significant difference firms will shift business to the cheapest of the three means of transport. If this bill is passed it is sure to cause a rise in shipping costs. Transport minister Jack Davis of British Columbia, for example, estimates that this measure could mean increases of 30 per cent for rail and marine shipping. Salt from Nova Scotia mines will be put at a comparative disadvantage, for example, with Rumanian salt. Worst of all-and this could be disastrous for Cape Breton-it could mean a cancellation of the steel complex for Cape Breton because of increased shipping costs and the fact that it will be cheaper to process Canadian ore abroad rather than in the Atlantic area.
What about rail passenger transportation? If the government was really interested in presenting this country with a useful transportation policy, now is the time to call for hearings to find out what the people of Canada want and need. However, instead of having people involved in planning a new transportation strategy for Canada, we have them reacting to a three-page outline by the Canadian Transport Commission on alternative cutbacks in passenger service from Montreal to points west. We are offered no supporting papers which deal with the social or over-all economic costs of these measures. There is nothing at all. These are hearings held in a vacuum.
In the meantime, the railway companies are allowed to cut back services. The CNR is dropping one of its transcontinental trains this summer, when the Olympics will be on and when people will need to be moved across this country. While waiting for the government to develop a policy, the Minister of Transport has ordered the companies not to purchase any more rail passenger equipment. The CNR is retiring 50 passenger rail cars, which will amount to 15 per cent of its passenger capacity. When it comes to improving Canadian rail passenger service, all this seems to come under Professor Parkinson's third law which states that delay is the deadliest form of denial.
In my opinion, policy formation is the responsibility of the people's elected representatives, not the role of appointed individuals in the CTC, and even when the government does decide to improve rail service it does so in the most absurd way. For example, let us look at the recent government decision to give the CPR $30 million to upgrade its service between Montreal and Quebec City. Canadian Pacific has never indicated any interest in rail passenger service in the corridor between Quebec City and Montreal. It is the CNR which has shown the people of Canada that it is interested in passenger service. The CNR
Transportation Policy
has shown an interest in improving rail passenger service, but the CNR did not get the $30 million.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just say that you adorn the chair very well, and you appear to be a person with the impartiality we in this House would like. Of course, we have received that from Mr. Speaker, but you seem to fit into that chair very well and I am glad to see you sitting in that place.
In view of the fact that our time is limited, I would like to start off my remarks by complimenting the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) on the very important motion he has brought to the attention of the House. This motion is of great concern to a good number of people in our country, dealing as it does with matters relating to transportation, a most important topic in a country the size of Canada.
I am sorry that the minister is not able to be here this afternoon for this very important debate, but I see that his parliamentary secretary is here. I am sure that in his usual way he will take notes and relate all the information which comes from this side of the House to the minister in the hope that it will have some effect upon him. I am sorry to say that during the time the minister has been in his portfolio he has not taken advice or had the consultation which I think is expected of a minister of transport in an area which has been referred to-and was referred to again today-by the minister's predecessor, as being a mess.
I listened with great interest to the minister's comments today relating to his theory and his concept of transportation in Canada. Much of what he said is quite true. I say that in the spirit of attempting to have a dialogue with the minister relating to transportation matters in Canada. I think it is most important that this matter be dealt within a non-partisan debate. It should be dealt with in a debate without partisan consideration, in which there could be consensus throughout the land. I commend that attitude to the minister.
I hope the minister will change his present attitude with respect to developing transportation policies in Canada, because the evidence we have before us is that he is making, not only piecemeal decisions before coming to any firm conclusion with respect to transportation policy for Canada, but he is doing so without the benefit of full consultation with those involved in transportation. I think the example of transcontinental rail passenger service, mentioned by the member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), is a good one. That is an area in which the minister has not carried out discussions across Canada. Rather, he has given a directive to the CTC with respect to a policy to be implemented, an irreversible policy, and he has sent the CTC out under the guise of consultation when everyone knows that the die is cast in that regard.
I am not alone in suggesting that the minister is instituting a transportation policy of his own which is on a piecemeal basis. A very respected spokesman for western agriculture, in the person of E. K. Turner, president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, saw fit to put out a press

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
release recently in which he pointed out that the minister has in fact been instituting his own transportation policy. He has not done so in any co-ordinated way but, rather, on a piecemeal basis and no one knows for sure whether one part will fit with the others. Mr. Turner condemns the government for operating in that fashion. Therefore, I hope the minister will heed some of the criticism from very responsible people across Canada and give a little more thought to getting some advice from people who have knowledge and expertise in the area of transportation, as well as from people who are affected by changes in transportation policy.
In concluding this part of my remarks, I want also to remind the minister that, as I understand it, he made a commitment to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications that the committee would have the full responsibility of investigating national transportation policy. As I understood the minister, he would not be introducing any policies with respect to transportation until the committee had had a full opportunity to investigate the subject. I am sorry to say that what we have had in committee has been, almost exclusively, representations and submissions by officials of the department. On a limited basis we had a number of opportunities to deal with certain aspects of transportation, notably through a trip to the west coast recently.
Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary seems to indicate another position, but I am sure he will have an opportunity to make a speech this afternoon. I have to make a confession, Mr. Speaker. It is an awful thing to have to say, but I must bare my soul. The parliamentary secretary is a former student of mine. To paraphrase the Prime Minister's remark: Where have I gone wrong?
I want to address my remarks primarily to the area of rail passenger service. Here is an example of the kind of ill-considered policy that has been rammed down our throats without full consultation and an opportunity to consider its implications for the people of Canada. I find that policy incredible for any minister of transport, but particularly incredible for a minister from western Canada. I have referred to the fact that the former minister of transport, now the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand), referred to transportation in Canada as being in a mess. He was not kidding, Mr. Speaker. I do not think the extent of this mess was revealed to us in the statement made by the present minister about the federal government's new rail passenger policy at the end of last January.
In introducing the policy, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) said that although Canada has extensive rail passenger services, they have been allowed to deteriorate so that Canadians no longer have a fair incentive to use them. He added that this was in no way due to any fault on the part of those who operate the trains, but to a combination of management and government policies which could only produce losses and worsening service. Losses, according to the minister, amounted to $167 million in 1974 and are increasing. He went on to say that losses may amount to $400 million by 1980 if changes are not made.
This sounds like a very ominous forecast. But what are the facts? The Department of Transport, in my estimation,
[Mr. Hnatyshyn.l
seems to have a bias against passenger rail. Like bees to honey, they swarm around glamour projects such as STOL, the short take-off and landing aircraft. The government has spent over $150 million on STOL, the heavily subsidized "new baby", only to have Mr. Kirkwood, the senior assistant deputy minister, inform me and my colleagues on the transport committee in February that they have no idea what to do about STOL now that the demonstration project is over. What we are witnessing is another hydrofoil case which involved a loss to our taxpayers of $52 million spent on a vessel designed to carry passengers over water at fast speeds, the Bras d'Or which now sits propped up and dejected on the shore at Halifax as a very expensive wallflower.
The Minister of Transport states that rail passenger service does not pay its way, therefore rationalization is needed. In the department's terms, "rationalization" is defined as "reductions". Why is it that a government which sinks $400 million into the Pickering airport and then suspends its construction, gags over a $160 million loss on rail passenger services? There are many examples of areas where the federal government picks up losses and deficits with respect to essential services. For example, the government picks up the $26 million annual deficit incurred by the Canadian National cargo and ferry service on the coast of Newfoundland.
A research study shows that Canada lags five years behind the United States, ten years behind the United Kingdom, and 20 years behind France in new rail passenger service concepts. The same study shows that passenger trains in Canada are "almost always late" and that rail operations in Canada are "more dangerous than other systems", recording, in 1972, 12 times more derailments and three times more collisions per train mile, twice as many passenger deaths and 17 times the number of rail employee deaths and injuries than France, for example.
Although the federal government is just beginning to admit it, the Canadian public has been aware for years that our railway passenger transportation system is in a state of deterioration. Certainly, during my time in parliament we in the opposition have been pressing the government to develop a national transportation policy, including rail passenger service-a policy that would be integrated, less costly, workable and fair to all parts of the country. In June, 1975, the former minister of transport stated in his overview of policy proposals that transportation should be an instrument of economic and social development.
With special reference to rail transportation, section 18(1) of the Canadian National Railways Act states that the railways of the Canadian National Railways "are hereby declared to do works for the general advantage of Canada". The Minister of Transport, in a letter dated April 5, 1976, to His Worship Mayor T. J. Cavanagh of Edmonton, Alberta, stated that the rail passenger policy was put forward in explicit recognition of the key role that railway passenger services play, not only in the direct provision of transportation services but also in terms of employment, tourism and many other facets of the economies of all regions of Canada.
But the government's response to this date has been to submit the country to policy reversals dazzling in their frequency and continued ineptitude. Premier Alex Camp-
June 11, 1976

bell of Prince Edward Island has stated that the new policy statement on rail passenger service left him cold and confused. He found that the notion that the transportation system can serve as a development tool contradicted the idea that it could also be self-sufficient.
The government's entire transportation policy seems to be devoted to, and the Minister of Transport seems obsessed with, the "user pay" concept. This, I suggest, is one of the problems we face with this government: they only see things in black and white and have no flexibility in their approach to a transportation policy. There is absolutely no room for any deviation. Once the minister has in his mind that it is going to be a "user pay" concept, that means it will be a "user pay" concept whether it hurts or not.
The minister has referred to band-aid measures. He was trying to make us believe that the government is a brand new one and is going to cure all the woes of past years which got us into this mess by applying band-aids. Once you take them off, of course, it causes pain and suffering. Once the sores are exposed, they are susceptible to a kind of gangrene. That is what could happen to the transportation policy. It is the government's responsibility to act in a responsible manner, and not impose black and white concepts on us as these will have serious economic consequences.
I do not disagree with the "user pay" concept in the right circumstances, but what bothers me about the minister's approach is its inflexibility. The principle of "user pay" must be weighed against what I consider the more important policy principle-the principle that transportation is an instrument of national policy and a tool of regional development. In my view, the geographical distance of Canada makes residents of the different parts of this country remote from each other and an exception to the objective of commercial viability is necessary to allow rail passenger services to fulfil the role of linking this country. The previous minister of transport agreed to let the standing Committee on Transport and Communications review recent government studies.
I hear thunder outside, Mr. Speaker, and I know He is with us as well, bringing lightning down on the heads of the government.

The minister's statement was a dramatic reversal of the government's rail passenger
Transportation Policy
policy as enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on June 18, 1974, at Cornwall. I see the hon. member from Cornwall present in the House. He may remember the Prime Minister's glowing remarks which were instrumental, no doubt, in the hon. member's being elected to sit on the government side.
