speechtext: Now the Prime Minister's words are a millstone around his neck.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
On that occasion the Prime Minister did not mention any form of physical removal of passenger rail service: he promised, instead, as the hon. member no doubt remembers, additional services. A Canadian passenger corporation would be established by the government to operate all intercity passenger train services and to set up transcontinental excursion trains to supplement the existing cross-country services. That was quite a speech. I see the hon. member smiling, no doubt as he fondly remembers the Prime Minister's promises. The Prime Minister said that there would be increased provision on the transcontinental services of piggyback carriage of private automobiles so that persons taking the excursion runs could use their own cars at their destination.
The backtracking came quickly. To the Speech from the Throne of 1974, and the tabled statements on rail passenger policy, was added the sneaky proviso that transportation policy would be implemented within the means of the financial resources of the federal government. During the last federal election campaign the Liberal party did not mention in any way that transportation policies would be subject to financial restrictions.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that transportation is a top priority which should not be hindered by financial restraints or rationalization. I will not dwell on the discrepancy between government promises in the last election campaign and the reality of government transportation policy, but will add that the Prime Minister himself said during the last election campaign that Liberal promises would not be "pie in the sky." Now, on the minister's instructions, the Canadian Transport Commission is holding public hearings with a view to reorganizing the rail passenger system by 1980, dropping some duplicate services and improving operation in the heavily populated Quebec City-Windsor corridor. I contend that the government's true intention is not so much to reorganize our rail passenger service as to reduce substantially the service in some parts of the country or wipe it out completely.
The Minister of Transport's new rail passenger policy has created great apprehension throughout the land. To cite just one example, in his own city, Saskatoon, the city council passed an emergency resolution expressing disapproval of any proposal to reduce transcontinental rail passenger service. It expressed particular opposition to the reduction or discontinuance of any such service passing through Saskatoon.
The new, so-called self-sufficent policy announced by the Minister of Transport has run into considerable opposition, particularly in the maritimes and the west which will apparently feel the brunt of the new policy. I hope it is only a coincidence that the only area of Canada promised new initiatives and expenditures in rail passenger travel, the area between Quebec City and Windsor, is an area

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
largely represented by members of parliament supporting the government.
The minister says he must phase out non-profitable rail passenger service because too few people use trains and they are not paying their way. I disagree with the statement presented to the Canadian Transport Commission earlier this year that passengers have deserted the railways. I believe passengers were driven away by government policies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join other hon. members in appreciating your presence in the chair this afternoon. This day's debate is particularly interesting as it deals with the difficulties parliament and the government can encounter in bringing about needed changes and in changing old ideas. Of course, change runs counter to Tory philosophy, perhaps best expressed by a Tory in Great Britain, whose name escapes me, who said, "Any change at any time, for any reason, is to be deprecated."
The minister has taken on a massive job in looking into the history of his department. He is examining a mass of regulatory sacred cows and is determined to change at least basic principles, even if some things are not to be changed overnight. He has suggested that the cost of this enormous transportation apparatus should be borne fundamentally by users unless a good case can be made to the contrary. This does not mean that there are not instances throughout the country, possibly in every constituency, calling for subsidy and assistance. But the basic argument proposed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is unassailable, I suggest.
The minister asks, "Why should someone be given a free or a subsidized rate, at the expense of someone else, if that situation can be corrected without endangering the fundamental economic viability of the area in question? He suggests, also, that it is more sensible to subsidize directly an area in which the assistance will do the most good. These policies show the minister to be tough but farsighted. If Canadian transport policy is in a mess, as has been alleged, or in difficulty, the surest way to create order is by applying the kinds of solutions he has recommended.
Numerous examples respecting the transportation question have been cited. I think the most graphic one drawn by the minister showed that bus travellers pay for their service entirely; automobile passengers are subsidized at the rate of .5 cent per mile; air travellers at 2 cents per mile, and rail travellers at 6 cents per mile. The minister asks, "Is it fair to ask the bus traveller to pay his fare and a portion of the train traveller's fare as well?"
Let me say a word about airports. There is a major airport in my constituency. Airports are extremely costly facilities. The government has been criticized for allowing airports in the past to be built without considering, first, efficient use and convenience of passengers who must use them. Too often, airports have been built as large entertainment centres, where people see travellers off or greet them. This has created enormous parking problems.

The "user pay" principle, as far as it relates to federal government airports and related aviation facilities, is aimed at placing a fairer share of the cost of the burden on the shoulders of that section of the Canadian public which benefits most from the use of any particular transport facility. For instance, it is well known that only between 10 per cent and 15 per cent of our population actually use our aviation facilities. The cost of building and maintaining these facilities has increased at an incredible steadily growing rate in recent years. At the same time, the government is keeping well in mind that the cost of certain aviation facilities, such as those in the Arctic, should continue to be borne by the public, or the taxpayer. In that category also come such things as government support for airport development and improvements which may be part of a regional economic development program, the provision of airport facilities and services for remote regions and other, similar regional and national undertakings.
The framework for user charges was provided for in the National Transportation Act of 1967 in which it was stipulated that each mode of transport in Canada, as far as was practicable, should bear a fair proportion of the real costs involved in providing that mode of transport. It can be shown that in 1976 or 1977 the Department of Transport's air transportation administration will be seeking parliamentary approval of a non-budgetary appropriation totalling some $385 million, as well as approximately $75 million in increased loan authority to support the international airports at Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Therefore, the total air program will be around $460.7 million.
The deficit in the next fiscal year has been estimated at $225.3 million. Because of the burgeoning costs of operating our aviation facilities, a number of user fee charges have been introduced this year. These include a 30 per cent increase in national fees and an increase from $33 to $50 per flight in respect of using North Atlantic facilities. I will not go into further detail. I do not think this is of particular interest beyond stating that it is a specific major example where, notwithstanding an increase in user fees, the Canadian taxpayers, 85 per cent of whom do not have anything to do with flying, are paying a very large proportion of this cost. Those of us who travel regularly by air are the beneficiaries. What the Minister of Transport is saying is that as a basic, underlying principle of policy, the user should pay in full for the product he is using unless it can be demonstrated that a wider public interest dictates otherwise.
In the United States, many major airports have been built, with the airlines being obliged to subscribe to the bond issues that finance the construction. The price that they pay is high, but this is compensated by the fact that they can dictate to a large extent how the airports will be laid out and how they will be most efficiently utilized. In this country we have a different procedure. I am gratified to find that in this area and in others citizens who use the facilities, or those companies who ship the products, must be prepared to pay.
We see throughout government that one of the problems is that history may have baked our cake, as someone once said. We in this parliament must be prepared, not in this area of government alone but in many others, to consider
June 11, 1976

that while the programs as formulated were adequate and proper at the time, they may require change. We should not build up sacred cows, unchangeable objectives, and rebel when positive reform is offered. If we run up large annual deficits in this country, a good proportion of them are borne by projects which have served their purpose and are now in need of reform and scaling down. This is true right across the board, whether it be unemployment insurance, health costs or transportation. If we are wedded to programs, we will not make the reforms or changes which would deprive the people for whom they were designed, but will make them more efficient and reduce the cost to the taxpayers.
I fail to see why every time a policy is proposed to parliament which has as its objective saving the taxpayers money without impairing the program, the Tories in particular turn on the minister who brings them forward, even though they would reduce the impact and burden of government financing, freeing moneys for other purposes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
When that politician was stuck for a source of fact, he always had a phrase in his speech which was,
Transportation Policy
"Grisdale says". That was his source of reference. Grisdale was a man who had a great capacity for knowledge and was famous for many sayings. The hon. member for Mississauga, in his reference to the Tories, was using a "Grisdale". He was not using a Tory, nor was he quoting directly from anybody; he was merely attacking-and that is his prerogative.
Every member of this House recognizes that there must be change. It is not simply the characteristic of the government, the Conservatives or the NDP. Every person, regardless of his political philosophy, recognizes that our transportation system, which literally built this country, must now be adapted to fit what it built. Change we must support, but change must make for the better. It must not add to the confusion. This is what a multitude of Canadians fear as change is proposed at this moment in time in the transportation structure.
The policy as outlined this morning by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is purely theoretical. Scientists may sit down and rely on the law of gravity. They may rely on the laws of mathematics and may be accurate in the conclusions as they calculate solutions to the problems that face them, because those laws are inflexible and continuous; they are dependable. However, when one starts to deal with something such as the laws of economics and modes of transportation, one finds oneself in an entirely different situation where a single, simple formula does not fit the needs of the people to be served. Such in the case in the field of transportation: it is theoretical; it is not realistic.
Let me cite an example. The minister stated this morning that we should not be moving grain by rail in Canada; we should, instead, be exporting beef. Theoretically, this is a perfectly good statement; but in fact we are not competitive, in world markets, in beef. Most of the time we are not quite self-sufficient in beef products. It is therefore ridiculous to discuss the idea of turning corn into beef to sell, for example, to Italy, a country which could not afford to pay for it anyway.
Our farmers could not possibly live on the return for beef which the world market would bring us. I can envisage, too, that if we entered this trade our competitors would cut the price under us. On the markets of this continent, yes, our producers could survive although they have gone through hard times, but on the markets of the world we are really not competitive.
If we were to follow the pattern the minister suggests we would certainly dislocate a number of the economic structures which exist in this country, not only in the West and in the Atlantic area. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), the economy of certain areas depends to a very large extent on the system of railway rates presently in existence. The existence of these arrangements allows those sectors of the economy to remain in business, whether it be the apple growers of Nova Scotia, the wheat farmers of the prairies, or those who grow vegetables in central Canada; they depend upon their ability to get their goods to market at reasonable cost of transportation related to the weight and value of the produce.

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
The minister's theory breaks down because he fails to take into account the aspect of competition and the abnormalities which exist in the rate structure. I could give a number of examples, but again I will refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt. He pointed out that far too many rates are now based on what the traffic will bear; they are in no way related to compensation for the service rendered.
The mess which was described by a former minister of transport is one which was created by the party which has been in power in Canada virtually uninterrupted for 50 years, so when the present minister referred to band-aid solutions he was referring to the band-aid solutions applied by his predecessors. When he referred to decisions taken for political reasons he was referring to decisions taken by his predecessors-and in somewhat uncomplimentary terms. The policy which is in operation today is not a Conservative policy nor is it an NDP policy. It is a Liberal policy, and it has been for 50 years.
There is a fourth reason why the minister's suggestion that transport be placed on a user pay basis will not work out. I defy him to say to the urbanites of Montreal, Ottawa or Winnipeg, "You will pay the full cost of transportation in your city." It simply would not work. And just as it would not work in the urban areas, it would not work in the rural areas and all points between. No government anywhere has been able to make an airport pay for itself. There will be subsidies.
Let me turn to the Seaway. The minister spoke in deprecatory terms with respect to subsidies and those who rely upon them-it was the phrase "those who rely upon them" which some of us found offensive, and I might add that the objections did not all come from the Atlantic area. There is, by legislation, a subsidy paid to the maritime region under a measure known as the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Relate this to the Seaway.
The Seaway was opened in 1959. The fee structure was established in such a way, we were told, that not only would it pay for maintenance costs but it would amortize the cost of construction and, in the end, not cost Canadian taxpayers a nickel. Mr. Speaker, I submit that if the total investment in the Seaway were added up today one would find that this undertaking owes the Canadian people a billion dollars, and if this were to be financed in today's terms the amount of money paid to the Atlantic area would be less than 25 per cent of the interest charges alone on the amount of money the Seaway owes Canadians. Is the minister prepared to say to the City of Montreal, for example, "You will pay the actual cost of operations on the Seaway?" Try that one on for political size.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What about Saint John?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
We will come to that, all in good time. Here are at least three instances in which the user pay concept could not possibly be applied to the nth degree, even politically.
There are other instances which might be mentioned. Sacred cows? Political realities? They may be more than that. There may be economic realities, and they may in the end be in the interest of the nation. I do not really agree with the idea that the federal government should be paying subsidies to any part of Canada. But if there are not

to be subsidies, let me point out right away that the anomalies in freight rates which we were supposed to get rid of long ago, according to the former minister of transport, still exist. For instance, there is the $90 rate to Nickel Belt referred to a little while ago, as compared with the $45 rate for iron pellets to Pittsburgh. These are anomalies we cannot afford. Cannot we obtain rational rates which relate to the ton-mile cost, or the cost the shipper or the consumer can bear? Let us change the system by all means, but change it in a way which will bring about a better transportation structure, one which will be of benefit to the total economy.
Criticism has frequently been expressed about what is happening to passenger service. In the past 50 years or so the government never paid serious attention to the service which was being rendered by the railroads as passenger service was being phased out. I am sure that you, Mr. Speaker, have had the same experience as I had when I waited three hours in the bowels of the station in Windsor in trying to get a connection between the passenger service of the CPR and the CNR in Nova Scotia. I have waited overnight in the City of Saint John to get from train to boat although both are operated by the same company. I have driven my car-something the minister deplores- because I knew I would not be able to get to Saint John by the passenger service provided and complete my business without having to stay in that city overnight. With that timetable, Mr. Speaker, the operation had to fail.
One of the factors which contributed to the disappearance of express and passenger service was the removal of mail contracts. This has proven to be a sorry decision as far as the effect upon mail delivery is concerned. In former times mail to the east was often delivered over night. It is a rare occasion now, under the present airmail system, for a piece of mail to be delivered over night to my constituency. And so it has been during that period of 50 years under the Liberal administration that this system has gone downhill in every aspect, whether it be freight, passenger or express. It is the only system, Mr. Speaker, in which government has permitted excessive charges for deteriorating services. And the government opposite sat back and watched it happen.
Not too long ago the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) moved a motion in the House with respect to the conditions of the railways in Prince Edward Island. There are no other means of transportation services leaving that island other than rail services. Yet the railroad is in a condition which is unacceptable, deplorable, and incapable of giving proper service to the area. That has happened under 50 years of Liberalism, with a little interruption under the guidance of a Crown corporation. It is no use government trying to avoid the responsibility.
Let me come back to another user pay concept. Bill C-61 has been proposed by the Government of Canada. It is a notable bill and I for one support the principle that Canada should have a merchant marine. No matter what I may say in criticism of that bill, Mr. Speaker, bear in mind that this is my principle and my objective just as much as that of any person inside or outside the House. However, we come back to a theoretical position on the bill presented to the
June 11, 1976

House; we have ignored the practical situation that exists in the economic world in which the act would take effect.
Let me remind the House of some of the comments that have been made but whose authors have not been given the opportunity of presenting their case before the committee or the House. I have before me a telegram from the Atlantic premiers conference, signed by Mr. A. B. Campbell. I wonder who he could be? I think he is the Liberal premier of the province of Prince Edward Island. I will not quote this telegram in full because I do not have time, but it says this in part:
Existing industry and future industrial development in the Atlantic provinces will be seriously affected if this bill, and those regulations of which we have been made aware to date, come into effect.
That telex was dated May 26 last and was directed to the Minister of Transport. Has the telegram been acknowledged, Mr. Speaker? There are those who do not know whether it has. In any event that is the position of the Atlantic provinces.

There are none so blind as those who will not see. Let us just see, Mr. Speaker, how all this began. We are all fully aware of the Darling report. A multitude of people in the Atlantic area made representations to the group that made the report. Their objections did not appear in the report, nor were they given consideration in the economic conclusions that the report reached.
A meeting was held in camera in Halifax between federal and provincial officials and industry and labour representatives in regard to the Darling report on July 18, 1973. Here is a list of the people who appeared. First of all the provinces made an appearance and their representative said it had been agreed with the then minister, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand), that no action would be taken until the regulations were approved by the provinces.
The Sydney Steel Corporation said the Darling report would hurt them. The Canadian Salt Co. did not favour it because it would hurt them. Dover Flour Mills suggested that they might have to close. Gulf Oil Company were going to have problems. Labrador Linerboard said they were threatened with loss of business. The Maritime Cooperative Services spoke on behalf of the farmers and said that the increased cost of farm requirements would be severe, and they objected. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission presented a brief rejecting the principles as outlined. Smith Brokerage, which deals in grain, said the cost of the proposals would affect the Atlantic area, and they objected.
The pertinent part of the minutes of this meeting is as follows. Labour union opinion-I understand this came from the SIU-was this:
The two representatives expressed their agreement with the recommendations of the Darling report. Noting: the lack of a real national transportation policy; that the government should provide the vessels that are required to move the cargoes-
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when the corporations complained about the costs that they feared and anticipated, the union recognized, as well as the corporations, that such an act without subsidy would be nothing but detrimental
Transportation Policy
to the manufacturing and shipping industries of the Atlantic area. I repeat that I favour the formation of a Canadian merchant marine, but it must not be a theoretical thing of the sort the minister talked of this morning; it must be practical in every sense of our economic world. One shipper suggested to the transportation committee in Vancouver that if the government would offer tax incentives or other incentives comparable with those given to ships of foreign registry, it might be possible to have in Canada a merchant marine that could operate and have a chance to profit; but the government has said it would not care to do this. I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the union representatives recognized fully that this could only happen with government assistance or through incentive of one form or another, even if it supplied the ships to the shippers.
The Halifax Chronicle-Herald for May 19 said that financial incentives are required to encourage a Canadian flag fleet. The Gazette for Tuesday, May 25, carried the headline, "Atlantic Provinces Concerned Over New shipping Act Changes". I could go on to read these editorials, Mr. Speaker, but there just is not time.
Let me come back to the user pay concept. Again the Chronicle-Herald has an editorial from which I wish to quote briefly:
With major markets in the centre of the country, producers in the east and west are placed at a competitive disadvantage .. .
Government simply is determined that there are two classes of users and that one class is to have preferential treatment.
The currently popular policy favours the heart of the country and greatly strengthens the Ontario economy. The price is paid by the west and the east.
That is where the political clout is which the minister was talking about this morning. I should also like to refer to the Halifax Chronicle-Herald for Monday, May 3, 1976. I want to quote a name familiar to the government of the day, Premier Regan, who in this article criticized the program. Then I want to refer to another chap who is familiar to the government of the day, Mr. Jack Davis from B.C. According to the article:
Mr. Davis said last week that the amendments would force shippers to wait for a Canadian flagship to carry his goods if one were available immediately. Premier Regan said if Mr. Davis ran the B.C. transport department the way he ran the federal fisheries department "it's quite possible he could be mistaken."
I like that little comment.
The Gazette for Tuesday, May 25, carried this headline: "Merchant Marine Policy-Cost-Benefit Focus of Study". I want to refer to an article dealing with what members of the committee and those opposed to the act asked for consistently, and to which no one would respond until after the committee had risen and this little snippet appeared in the Gazette:
A key element in forming the recommendations will be a series of cost-benefit studies now under way-
This has neither been acknowledged nor denied by the government in regard to Bill C-61.
-Roland Murray, a senior adviser to the federal transport ministry, told a meeting of the Naval Officers' Association of Canada Montreal branch.
.. . Murray, who heads the board's working committee, said there can be no policy recommendations to the transport minister until the board sees the conclusions of 20 studies it has commissioned covering such

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
areas as international agreements, labour, shipping rates, and shipping in the Arctic.
Despite this statement by a high ranking official in the government, only as recently as last Wednesday the government was trying to rush this bill through by June 30. I suggest that we need the kind of change called for by the hon. member for Mississauga. Above all, one of the things we need is a change in the way policy decisions are reached, as well as a change in the way legislation is framed so that people may be guided in what they do. This Marine Code Act, including its most recently suggested amendment, is enabling legislation. It has "mays" and "mights" and permissions throughout both the act and the regulation. For this reason it leaves the people at the mercy of government policy at the moment in time at which a decision affecting industry is to be made. If that policy at that moment is unfavourable then industry will suffer the consequences.
I want to give one assurance to the minister while I am in the process of these remarks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some rather specific points to make with regard to the subject of this opposition day.
One of the major transportation problems of our country is the establishment of a rational, efficient, and flexible system for the shipment of grain from the prairie provinces to Canada's ports and then overseas to our export markets. While this is an issue of interest to all Canadians, it is of particular concern to those of us in the western part of this country, whether in the prairie provinces where the grain is produced, or in British Columbia where we haye had, at the same time, the most attractive and effective delivery system, and the greatest problems in making that particular system work.
Over the past eight years the volume of overseas grain exports shipped through west coast ports has fluctuated between 37 per cent and 57 per cent of total Canadian grain

exports. On the average the three western grain ports, Vancouver, Victoria, and Prince Rupert, have handled 45 per cent of overseas grain exports, yet these three ports have a total storage capacity of under 27 million bushels while the 30 terminals in eastern Canada have a capacity of over 141 million bushels, that is, five times as great.
I point this out to hon. members not only as a tribute to our current system of western grain exports and to the men and women who make it work, but also as an indication of what can be done if this western system is properly rationalized and suitably upgraded. Two steps in this direction, which I am pleased to note have recently been taken, are the Canadian Wheat Board's program to expand significantly west coast grain storage capacity, and the visit last month by the Transport and Communications Committee to western Canadian communities to study at first hand problems such as those being outlined here today.
One of the visits by the transport committee was to the port of Prince Rupert where members met with a number of local representatives, including Mr. Joe Scott, chairman of the Prince Rupert Port Authority, and the city of Prince Rupert grain co-ordination committee represented by Mayor Lester and Dr. William Hick. I am confident that the members of this committee have returned from their western trip convinced, as I am, that the key to the rationalization and expansion of the western grain exporting system is the port of Prince Rupert.
The problems of shipping grain through Vancouver are numerous and have been discussed in this House on more than one occasion. The advantages of Prince Rupert, however, are just now beginning to be realized. The current single grain elevator in Prince Rupert is owned by the Canadian Grain Commission of the Department of Agriculture, and is currently undergoing a three-year renovation and structural upgrading program. In addition, a facility study is currently being conducted to determine the possibility of increasing the storage capacity of this particular elevator. This study, I am certain, will bring back a positive report.
What is needed to rationalize western grain shipments is a greater utilization of lower volume rail lines; better usage of existing port facilities; an increase in storage capacity in areas where rail congestion and land prices do not make such a step impossible; a more wisely regulated pattern of ship movements; a full recognition of the strategic location of B.C. ports and their relative closeness to Pacific markets; and full co-ordination of the plans and activities of the several federal government departments and agencies involved in the western export of grain.
The first five points can all be facilitated by an increased use of the grain exporting facilities of the port of Prince Rupert. The sixth is already becoming a reality under the more than capable stewardship of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
As the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has indicated by his motion today, it is after all not really a grain problem that we are discussing. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am indebted to the hon. gentleman for raising this exceptionally relevant topic of interest to every Canadian, and I think particularly relevant to those who are regionally
June 11, 1976

disadvantaged. As a representative of such an area I feel it is important that this sense of regionality be communicated in this House.
In utilization of the ports in my area and, ports not being the only subject, also the utilization of present rail and other transportational infrastructures, we are an adolescent part of the world. Although we are mature in years, utilization has been, to use the minister's word, immature. Ever since the original building of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railroad, which was finally joined in 1912 with the "last spike" at Fort Fraser, in the centre of the constituency of Skeena, our northern half of British Columbia has been overwhelmingly concerned with transportation, and we have been eternally cognizant of the unequal battle that must be waged not only west to east but, similarly, north to south, as we have seen a giant concentration of traffic funnel first to the east, and then an even greater volume south through Vancouver and its environs.
Our CN northline-Edmonton to Red Pass, Red Pass to Prince George, and Prince George to Prince Rupert- seemed to languish, only partially utilized, although it has been acknowledged over and over again as economic and even superior in assessment of coal shipping potential-in fact just the other day I observed an article by an expert on unit trains who said it was possible to deliver grain at $10 a ton to only two ports in Canada, and I am sure the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) will be as happy as I am to know that one of those ports is Halifax and the other is the port of Prince Rupert.
In the transportation of minerals, for instance, the capacity of a rail route from mine to port is gauged by the "ruling grade"; that is, the most severe grade a train must pass on a given line. In the case of all southline traffic from Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia to southern ports, severe grades in the mountains require up to ten 3,000 horsepower locomotives to do what four can do on the CN northline. In addition transport over these reduced grades permits a significant increase in the tonnage that is carried.
In 1976, the CN has scheduled a $100 million capital budget for the mountain region alone. This represents 25 per cent of all capital outlays planned, including equipment, in the whole country. Part of this is for expanded terminal facilities in Vancouver and Edmonton, including two 12-mile sections of double track on the southline. CN anticipates an 80 per cent increase in tonnage in Canada over the next five years. Where will that put us? Double tracking becomes necessary above 35 trains per day. We are certainly a long way from that at the current rate of five trains a day. Estimates are that by 1990 Prince Rupert to Prince George traffic will be up to between eight and ten trains per day, and Prince George to Red Pass will be somewhere between 15 and 19. Now let us take a look at what those trains are or may be carrying in the future.
In the two years between 1972 and 1974 Canada's exports to Japan rose from $957 million to a record $2,220 billion. In imports, Canadians purchased $1,427 billion in producer goods, consumer durables, and non-durables including trucks, motorcycles, and the ever present Japanese cars. As well, a surprising new non-commodity trade is showing
Transportation Policy
strongly as a projected 85,000 Japanese tourists visited Canada in 1975. Eighty per cent of these visitors spent more than 24 hours in this country-and spent money! And they used transportation-air, train and cruiseship, as well as highway travel.
Development between us and our pacific neighbour is the most dynamic element among Canada's trading patterns. British Columbia, the Yukon and Northwest Territories have combined to lead exports with an amount of $1.18 billion in 1974, of which $462 million was copper and $309 million was forest products; these two commodities alone accounted for more than one third of all Canadian export earnings in Japan. A further 53 per cent of Canada's total exports to Japan in 1974 was from the two territories and B. C. You will note that I did not mention coal, which accounted for $229 million in that export basket.
Until the development of northeastern British Columbia coal properties by Utah mines, Dennison, Minolta and Quintette, coal is still mainly a southern B.C. product. Access is coming though to the new Alberta coal field developments such as those I have just mentioned, as well as Coalition Mining, Sukunka and Teck Corporation, and if they are proved viable and economic there will be further access required under the transportation policy.
Last November the government completed an agreement regarding northern railway transportation which would have seen the access improve considerably because of the necessity for resource transportation. I say "would have seen" because this agreement is stalled, even though it generated considerable heat and light-not much light- last December during the B.C. provincial election. We now have the minister of transport for B.C.-whom many members of the House will remember, and whom indeed I remember very well as being the first to quote widely the $1 per ton saving in shipping coal through the CN northline-now seeming to do another about face and seeing in BCR access to Squamish another possibility. I can only hope that we northern British Columbia citizens will not have to live through another protracted political battle with the B.C. railway port of Squamish, and that economics and good sense, and not just politics, will prevail.
The proposed BCR Dease Lake sharing, which would have seen the federal government pay British Columbia $117.5 million in return for a one third sharing of the cost of construction of the CN northline from Terrace to Sus-keena, has met with rejection from the new B.C. government, and so it is back to the drawing board again with a recommencement of negotiation. These transportation linkages are essential for and inseparable from the economic enhancement of northern B.C., and I am pleased to note that the federal Minister of Transport will soon meet with his opposite number in B.C. All I can say to Jack Davis is, "Your new government is now six months old and it is time to get on with the job." We await provincial planning priorities and we await impatiently in northern British Columbia the infrastructure that the north lacks in order that we might become equal partners with the south of our province.
The precedent has been established in Fort Nelson where millions of DREE dollars have been invested in municipal services, notably in sewer systems to the betterment of the community and enhancement of back-up services to indus-
14434

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
trial expansion. If we cannot get B.C. "off the pot" in a reasonable amount of time, then I say, scrap the present agreement, formulate a new transportation and regional development co-ordinated federal policy and go it alone, if we must, to allow regionally deprived areas to survive these troubled times. I say, please do not keep the northern half of this country waiting any longer. Regionally deprived areas need transportation access in order to survive in troubled times, and in my view there are some towns and villages which cannot continue to endure without the implementation at an early date of the subsidy assistance in transportation mentioned by the minister today.
What are we as a nation selling? What does Canada move to market in exports? We export agricultural products and we have a rising market in pork. We export coal, aluminum, zinc, iron, fertilizers, and manufactured goods, furs, radar equipment, power driven hand tools, perfumes, cosmetics, art, antiques and collector's items, and do not forget our tourist trade. We provide ski trips to the Rockies and other western trips which are becoming increasingly important. I remind hon. members that tourism is a labour intensive finished product and a renewable resource, as well as a non-environmentally damaging industry. Quite apart from visitor traffic, there are new transportation linkages and the general cargo terminal at Prince Rupert now awaiting phase three final finishing with a target date for opening in November of this year. Neptune terminals is presently proving the viability of the bulk loading facility at Ridley Island near Prince Rupert which will have further impact on western trade opportunities.
Northwestern British Columbia is not just Prince Rupert. The potential of Kitimat as a complementary resource oriented port is seriously being investigated by other private investors. Recent Kitimat development oriented proposals included a Nippon-Kokan steel mill, and presently Trans-Mountain Pipelines Limited and the Ashland Oil Company are proving the viability of a mid-province oil pipeline. This is one that brings a great deal of concern for a well balanced environmental approach, but in addition to that a very healthy concern that the economic benefits accrue to the area affected by the development of the pipeline. It really does not matter whether it is a pipeline or a grain elevator. The area which is providing the resource has a need to receive the benefits from such a development. These areas require the support of the engineering arm of this government, namely, the transportation facilities.
To the north above Kitimat and Prince Rupert, adjacent to the start of the Alaskan panhandle is the once bustling gold town of Stewart, a place where it is reported that once some 4,000 people lived when it was a gold town. This border area now includes less than 750 souls whose destiny is tied to the illusive price of copper. It is another port probability, another area which is mature and historic but which could benefit mightily from the sensitive administration of the policy the minister has so clearly enunciated today of subsidization to areas as yet undeveloped which are developmentally in need of transportation access to reach maturity and add to the productivity of this nation.
There is another hinterland in the northern part of B.C., the tenth National Harbours Board port in Canada for

Kitimat and Terrace and their untapped resources at this time. These future port, rail, road and communications linkages will, hopefully, bring the Yukon on stream again so far as Canadian transportation is concerned, bringing us back to greater utilization of our own facilities rather than the present practically economic and easily accessible Alaskan gateways of Skagway and Juneau. I look forward to the linking of Prince George through Watson Lake with the Mackenzie Valley as a development which common sense tells us must happen at some point in the not too distant future.
To perceive the world of the Pacific rim in all its variety I ask hon. members, this late Friday afternoon, to imagine a mathematics compass with Hawaii as your centre point. Inscribe a circle as broad as the world's biggest ocean. This Pacific circle has Alaskan and Russian shorelines to the north and west; there are China, Japan and a wealth of emerging and re-emerging small nations; further south are Australia and New Zealand, our Commonwealth neighbours. Then wing over to Antarctica, and eastwards up the coast of Chile and her southern hemisphere neighbours, Peru and Equador, to Central America, Mexico, the United States, and on to our home turf, the long coastline of British Columbia. This is the geography of future trade opportunities, each as potentially rewarding as the one we currently pursue with Japan.
To return to the specifics of mid-northern Canada and our B.C. requirements for greater transportation and communications access, the federal Department of Transport, under the leadership of the Minister of Transport, has initiated two areas of study which I predict will soon become household words in business and labour circles in every part of our nation.
Pacific Rim access is being studied first by the Department of Transport's policy planning and major projects branch to assess the effectiveness of transportation systems which carry exports to and from Pacific Rim markets. This MOT project affords a focus for three levels of government and the widely diffused array of Crown corporations, private entities, and agencies which comprise our access to the buyers of our goods and services.
Second, a task force is screening the gamut of transportation policies and has specifically delineated the need for alternate means of access to the west. This review forms part of the broad Pacific Rim access project and will profoundly affect us, particularly in western Canada, when completed.
Transportation and communications access are, in my opinion, the cornerstone on which our area's new economics must be built. We require a flexible system for the efficient shipment of grain; a fair recognition of third level air carriers and required subsidies, no matter where they operate in this nation; utilization of existing rail lines on economic rather than political bases; and regional transportation as an engineering arm of economic enhancement.
Reciprocal running rates are still being negotiated between the BC Railway and the CN and will have an enormous impact on the northern part of British Columbia when completed. The presently stalled CN line north from Terrace has received important impetus with the historic
June 11, 1976

commencement of tripartite land claims negotiation in the Nass Valley when the Nishga Tribal Council, the government of B.C., represented by the hon. Allan Williams, and the Government of Canada, represented by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), committed themselves to resolution of the Nishga's 111-year-old land grievance. This matter is now out of the hands of politicians and into the realm of professional negotiators. Progress on this front will signal the release of a log-jam of discontent which will make possible responsible development in the northern half of my province. Make no mistake, the Nishga people are not opposed to development; they simply seek to ensure their just participation in it, with benefits accruing to them from such development as it does to the non-Indian sector of our society.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will allow me one more minute.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate today on the user pay concept in transportation, and I would like to refer in my remarks to our national airline, Air Canada. I note that its president recently stated that he is going to be seeking a fare increase, so that the user is probably going to have to pay more to travel on Air Canada in the future. However, I am going to oppose this fare increase, and I have written Mr. Benson to notify him about the financial fiasco at the Air Canada finance branch in Winnipeg and the disastrous debt it is running up. Until this mess in Winnipeg is cleaned up there certainly should be no fare increase allowed for Air Canada.
There are other problems at the Air Canada finance branch, and these problems have been with the finance branch for over three years. One of them is a labour problem, and this related to job descriptions and overtime pay, and has nothing to do with poor accounting or auditing procedures.
For the last couple of months I have been asking that the Auditor General be directed to carry out a complete audit of the Air Canada finance branch and to establish a proper auditing and accounting system. This was recommended first by the Independent Review Committee which called for all Crown corporations to be audited by the Auditor General, and in the report it states:
The Auditor General should audit the financial accounts of all Crown corporations whose expenditures directly affect the budgetary accounts of Canada.
The budgetary accounts of Air Canada are certainly affected because I notice in Air Canada's annual report
Transportation Policy
this year that the federal government is giving Air Canada a donation of $5 million to build a hangar in Winnipeg. This is apparently a new procedure. In the past Air Canada had to build its own hangars, but now the government is contributing $5 million for a hangar in Winnipeg.
In addition, the Estey inquiry was established by the government to look into a $100,000 travel agency payment which Air Canada made. It was an improper payment, so the government had the Estey inquiry carried out at a cost of $400,000. If we are going to spend $400,000 to investigate a $100,000 payment, we should certainly have the Auditor General move into the Air Canada finance branch and carry out an audit there to investigate the fact that millions of dollars are going astray. I will get to that problem in just one moment.
In the Estey report it is stated;
As we have seen, the auditors of the Corporation are appointed by Parliament and are the same auditors as those appointed for the CNR. By Section 67 of the Financial Administration Act the Auditor Generral is eligible to be appointed as the Auditor or joint Auditor of the Corporation but such has not been done in the past.
So, the Auditor General has every right to move into the Air Canada finance branch to conduct an audit and to establish a proper accounting system.
In the Estey report it is stated that the market facts study was a bona fide research job but that the costs ran out of control as a result of a lack of monitoring by Air Canada personnel. All through the Estey report it is pointed out that there have been unauthorized disbursements, and a number of recommendations for improvements at the Air Canada finance branch are made.
I am sorry that the minister is not here today. I find it rather strange that on a transportation opposition day the minister is only here for a short period.

Wait until I get going, Joe. The parliamentary secretary is well aware of the problems at the Air Canada finance branch, as he has debated these problems with me on a number of occasions during adjournment debates. I find it very strange that the Minister of Transport has not given any constructive answers with regard to what he is going to do about these problems, and I hope that after today I can receive an answer from the parliamentary secretary as to what action will be taken to correct the problems at the finance branch.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) this week asked the Minister of Transport when Air Canada will be appearing before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, and I hope we can receive an answer today.
I would just like to go over some of the problems at the finance branch. I raised this matter with the Prime Minister on May 21.1 said to him:
I should like to point out to the Prime Minister that, since there are no longer any enforced controls on travel agents reporting ticket sales and, as of October, 1975, there were an excess of 96,000 unreported travel agent ticket sales, which represents a minimum of $2,208,000 unpaid for transportation,...
That is just one example, Mr. Speaker. If we can have the Estey inquiry because of a $100,000 transaction I think we had better get a little action on a missing $2 million. As I pointed out earlier, the President of Air Canada stated that he is going to need a fare increase. I hope the government will make sure that no fare increase is granted until the financial mess is straightened out.
I drew to the attention of the government that Air Canada's own internal auditors endeavoured to audit the refund bank drafts account in 1975. This account is not less than $2.5 million per month, about $30 million per year. They finally gave up and that account remains unaudited since 1972. Therefore over the past four years a $120 million account has been in question. When I bring matters like this up what do I get-"Do not talk about Crown corporations on the floor of the House." That is a lot of nonsense, Mr. Speaker. The government is obligated to take action when it has a mess like this on its hands.
I pointed out that a debt of $186,000 of Electronic Associates Canada Ltd. of Toronto had been written off. How could that be possible, Mr. Speaker? How could it be possible to run an account that high? You would think they would be alerted to it at about $20,000 or $25,000 and not let it go any further. I understand that all tickets have not been accounted for by this company and the debt could run much higher still.
I have pointed out that in the past Air Canada has broken IATA rules and regulations. They issued buyer vouchers to Tourist Mount Koyal, of Quebec, to the tune of $27,384. All that Air Canada collected from this travel agent was $9,445; they wrote off $17,938, Mr. Speaker. Under IATA rules and regulations this is illegal and the Auditor General should certainly look into it.
I also reported a letter from Harveys of Bristol (Overseas) Limited of London, England. They are continually complaining to Air Canada because they persist in paying the incorrect amount. Certain bills are overpaid and other accounts are not paid at all. As I pointed out, In the past the Air Canada Heathrow office in London has been threatened by the gas and light companies that the gas and

light will be shut off unless they pay their bills. Mr. Speaker, this is all because of the finance problems of Air Canada in Winnipeg, and it is another reason why the Auditor General should clean up this mess.
Another of Air Canada's strange practices is that of contracting out their work. The billing is being distributed to Office Overload in Vancouver, Montreal, and Toronto, and exorbitant sums are being paid for the work done which is coming back with a 50 per cent error factor. That means that they get into deeper trouble. The sooner this mess is straightened out the better. Most employees of the finance branch sit around doing very little work so it is strange that all this work is being contracted out. The minister should investigate the situation and find out why Air Canada is contracting work out, and put a stop to it. The cost ranges anywhere from $5,000 to $9,000 per week to individual companies.
I pointed out too, that there are in excess of 180,000 tickets which have been used but in respect of which there is no record of sales ever having been reported to the finance branch. At a dollar a ticket this represents a lot of money, but when one considers that the lowest charge on Air Canada flights is $23 there is cause for concern to the tune of a possible $3,843,000. Can anyone explain how many hundreds of thousands of ticket sales have been reported but in respect of which the fares collected are insufficient to cover the cost of transportation?
At the end of April this year Air Canada had a net loss of $141/2 million, about $l'/2 million over last year's deficit. We can see the direction things are going and why the government should get the Auditor General in to find out exactly what is going on. This should be done before Air Canada is brought before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. As was pointed out earlier, the Auditor General has authority to go in and conduct a survey.
Another area I should like to touch on is security at airports. We have reports that Air Canada has been warned by police that security is lax. An example is the gold robbery at the Ottawa airport. Air Canada was warned repeatedly by the Gloucester township police that there was no proper security. The gold theft a couple of years ago amounted to $175,000. To my knowledge there has been little or no improvement in security.
Another example is a group of Air Canada employees in New York who were arrested for alleged gold theft. I have been in touch with them and they tell me that security was removed a number of years ago and that they were in charge of large gold shipments themselves. These employees were arrested and charged with gold theft. They were eventually acquitted as they had nothing to do with the robbery, but they were left with legal fees of $18,000 which they had to pay themselves. This makes Air Canada employees or any airline employees very vulnerable. If there is any theft at any airport and employees are charged, Air Canada immediately dismisses them. They have to pay their own legal fees. I do not know why security was removed from these airports a couple of years ago, but the Minister of Transport should be looking into it. Apparently as an austerity measure Air Canada removed the guards at some of the airports. I fail to see the logic in that.
June 11, 1976

If an Air Canada employee is arrested the judicial system is so slow that his case could drag on for months, with legal fees mounting. They do not have any financial support from Air Canada.
In the few minutes remaining, Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate it if the parliamentary secretary would tell the House what action the government will take regarding the Air Canada finance branch and if he would comment on the matter of airport security.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to compliment the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) for bringing forward this motion today. I think it is the first time in the House of Commons that we have had an opportunity to discuss the user pay concept which is very important to all Canadians. They must have a full understanding of what the government is trying to do.
I heartily endorse the concept of the importance of transportation to regional disparities. I think it is most important to apply the cost-centre concept in letting the people of Canada know the purpose for which funds are to be used. If moneys are to be voted for regional disparity programs, let us account for them under such programs and not bury them in transportation estimates. It is important to eliminate the patchwork solutions to problems which are not aimed at eliminating problems but are designed to meet political situations. Put in simple economic terms I suggest that, by and large, it is better for the people who use the service to pay for it. I commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and his predecessor in that portfolio for having the political will to do what is right and to ignore political expediency in preparing our national transportation policy.
In any consideration of a cost effective, efficient transportation system you must remember that, if rates are low because of hidden costs, there will be greater use of expensive modes of transportation than there would be if fares or rates reflected real costs. That entails a loss to all.
This afternoon I should like to discuss the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. First, let me make a couple of com-
Transportation Policy
ments. I am continually surprised because members of the opposition, who preach government restraint and less government intervention in the private sector, want to maintain the present subsidy system and not make our transportation system self-sustaining, which is what the user pay concept advocates. These remarks also apply to the business community.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made his statement during the Christmas holidays on television, the business community was upset about his comments concerning the free market system. But when the business community discusses, for example, increased tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway system, it wants the tolls to remain the same. It does not want government intervention on the one hand, but likes the present subsidy system on the other. I remind the business community and the opposition that they cannot have it both ways.
Let me now speak about the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. It seems, because there has been so much talk of government restraint and so many questions about the effectiveness of government, that the press has not noticed something that happened in connection with the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. When the chairman of the St. Lawrence Seaway appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications I took note of the fact that administration costs in 1976 were lower than in 1973. In the past two years Seaway costs for maintenance, operations, and administration have risen only 12.8 per cent. I doubt if any government department, federal or provincial, any corporation, public or private, can boast of such a track record. That fact endorses, I think, what the Minister of Transport said earlier this afternoon. When the former minister of transport talked of the condition of this country's transportation system he was not referring to the managerial ability and effectiveness of those who operate this country's transportation systems.
It is important to reflect on the intent of the St. Lawrence Seaway Act, passed in 1951. It is also important to note that there was no opposition to certain clauses of the bill which were included at that time. For example, let me allude to section 17 which reads:
The tolls that may be charged by the Authority shall be fair and reasonable and designed to provide a revenue sufficient to defray the cost to the Authority of its operations in carrying out the purposes for which it is incorporated, which costs shall include
(a)	payments in respect of the interest on amounts borrowed by the Authority to carry out such purposes:
(b)	amounts sufficient to amortize the principal of amounts so borrowed over a period not exceeding fifty years; and
(c)	the cost of operating and maintaining the canals and works under the administration of the Authority, including all operating costs of the Authority and such reserves as may be approved by the minister.
Clearly, parliament's wishes have not been met. Some moments ago the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), a member of the transport committee for whom I have the greatest respect, commented on the government's band-aid approach. I remind him that in 1962 the Conservative government then in power eliminated tolls on the Welland Canal. That was a grandiose example of a band-aid approach to difficulties in transportation.
In 1959 the initial year of the Seaway operations, a tariff of tolls based on estimates of future traffic was established by agreement between Canada and the United States. Its

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
purpose was to obtain directly from the users the revenues required to cover operation and maintenance costs for this joint facility, as well as interest on loans and repayment of capital over a 50-year period.
From 1959 to 1973 combined revenues on the two sections had more than covered operation and maintenance costs but they were never sufficient to cover full interest or to enable any capital repayment. Since 1973, however, these costs have not been met and the annual deficit has been increasing steadily.
The main reasons why the original financial expectations were not fulfilled arise from circumstances which were not foreseen at the time the Seaway Authority's financial structure was established. Seaway tolls on the Montreal-Lake Ontario section have not been increased since the Seaway opened in 1959. Toll reviews took place in 1964 and 1967, but recommendations made by Canada to increase the level of tolls failed to obtain agreement on the part of the United States. Tolls on the Welland section of the system were suspended, as I said earlier, after an announcement in 1962 by the prime minister of the time.
The result has been that the Seaway's debt at the end of March of this year stood at $818 million. The difficult financial position in which the Seaway finds itself obscure, unfortunately, its true value to Canada as well as its operational success and over-all economic viability. Over 17 years of operations it has experienced a substantial growth in terms of tonnage. Long range forecasts of the traffic growth indicate a 12.5 per cent annual average increase during the next 15 years.
Many other benefits, including lowered transportation costs particularly on such key commodities to Canada as grain and iron ore, the development of increased international trade, and the impact on the labour and industrial sectors of the St. Lawrence River-Great Lakes area, have clearly established the Seaway's role as a vital element in our economy. Cabinet agreed some time ago that in principle the financial structure of the Seaway should be revised so as to provide the authority with a realistic financial base related to reasonable expectation of future revenues. The Minister of Transport has indicated his intention to recommend to his cabinet colleagues a revision that will have the added objective of providing a foundation for a new tolls policy.
Allow me to substantiate the benefits of the Seaway. Hon. members commented earlier about the importance of the Seaway with respect to the distribution of wheat. I remind hon. members that in 1958 the toll cost per bushel of wheat was 1.3 cents. In 1975 that cost, at 1.3 cents per bushel, remains the same. In other words, Mr. Speaker, between 1958 and 1975 the toll cost per bushel of wheat did not change. In addition, other costs during that period were increased.
The toll costs are not the reason for the increase in the price of wheat or other bulk products shipped through the Seaway. If I am not mistaken toll costs represented about 10 per cent of the sale price of a bushel of wheat in 1958. In 1975 those toll costs represented approximately 3 per cent of the sale price. Therefore tolls are an insignificant factor in total transportation costs, and form an insignificant part of the value of the merchandise when it finally reaches the consumer. The same may be said of coal and iron ore. The

toll costs for iron ore in 1965 represented about 9.5 per cent of the total transportation cost. In 1975 the proportion of tolls was reduced to 5.3 per cent, or almost half the previous amount. This again demonstrates the insignificance of the increase in tolls.
A moment ago I talked about the situation in the United States. Incidentally the situation in that country is the basis for the argument used by the business community and the opposition for the government's not increasing tolls. It is logical for our American Seaway counterparts not to want an increase in tolls. In 1970 Congress and the President of the United States enacted laws whereby all interest, both past and to be incurred in future, was to be written off. Consequently surpluses which the American authority had been able to generate were applied against some of the debt it had incurred. Let us consider the statement, made both by the American and Canadian authorities, that both countries benefit from the Seaway equally. We must assume that the Canadian government is picking up the majority of the deficit on the Welland Canal because it is 100 per cent Canadian-owned. What does this mean? It means that we are, in fact, subsidizing the Americans. Consequently the Americans have no incentive to increase tolls.
The cabinet agreed some time ago in principle that the financial structure of the Seaway should be divided in order to provide the authority with a realistic financial base related to reasonable expectation of future revenues. The Minister of Transport has indicated his intention to recommend to his cabinet colleagues a revision which will have the added objective of providing a foundation for a new tolls policy. Personally I do not think the government should write off the debt but change it into some form of equity because the Seaway does have substantial assets. The replacement cost is estimated at between $4 billion and $5 billion.
A policy of freezing Seaway tolls, and indeed an outright cancellation of these tolls, may be looked upon by some as a tool for promoting economic development. A serious drawback from Canada's point of view is that Canada carries more than 90 per cent of the investment and that our country bears a corresponding share of any deficits, while both countries benefit more or less equally from the waterway.
If we are to reach an explicit objective of commercial viability in terms of both the operations of the carriers and the provision of infrastructure, the St. Lawrence Seaway will no doubt have to be given a new financial structure and tolls will have to be increased.
This means that the users of the Seaway will have to pay to a reasonable degree the costs incurred in the operations of this transportation infrastructure. We must use sense and judgment to determine what a proper charge should be. Yes, the prices for transportation services will have to go up, and likely more rapidly than in the past.
It is the government's responsibility that the transportation system be efficiently run, that unjustified price increases are avoided, and that whatever increases are necessary are reasonable and equitable in terms of their impact. I heartily endorse the comments made by the hon.
June 11, 1976

member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to the effect that the onus is on each member of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, representing all sides of this House, to participate actively and constructively in meeting the request of the Minister of Transport to develop a new transportation policy for Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the debate on the motion moved today by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). It attempts to pinpoint some of the fundamental problems of transportation in this country. In particular it deals with the problem of the new concept of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) of user pay as it applies, in his words, to mature and immature regions in Canada and to the different modes of transportation.
Earlier today the minister graced us with some remarks. We are dealing with something that is fundamental to each member of this House, be he from the east, west, or central part of this land. It was rail transportation and some of the problems of transportation that built this country and helped keep it together. Coming from the Atlantic area and having practised law in British Columbia, I know something about the history of the CPR. Members from all parts of the country know how vital transportation is in terms of their allegiance to and identity with this country. That is why there is a very real concern in almost a non-political way when any new minister comes in with a so-called new policy.
When the minister starts referring to user pay, and to mature and immature regions of the country, opposition members, and I am sure some government members, would like to know just what he means. What do his officials mean when they talk about mature and immature regions of the land? Those are the words used in the minister's announcement of the policy.
If the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale) does not know that in the enunciation of the minister's policy the words "mature" and "immature" were used, I can understand why transportation in this country is in a mess. I hope that before time runs out today the parliamentary secretary will amplify, clarifly, or at least state what he means when he says I am misquoting when I talk about the mature and immature regions of this country in reference to the new transportation policy of his boss, the Minister of Transport.
The minister graced us today with an interesting lecture from the podium of the classroom on the problems in Canada and now we must be realistic.-I was going to give some very fundamental and detailed equations and figures with regard to some particular problems. However, when I heard the minister's dialectical exercise this morning I weighed upon the transport committee chairman on this side of the House to ask if I could reply to the minister. When the minister spoke today he tried to define his concept of user pay. In effect he made the brilliant statement that if the user does not pay, the non-user must. We have to be realistic in accepting this proposition. As I say, I am glad the hon. member for Crowfoot placed this motion before the House and that the minister was here this morning.
Transportation Policy
In Atlantic Canada we have had what was called transportation week. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary will have something to say about this. Even though the minister said he would be there to amplify on some of the problems of his new policy, unfortunately at the last minute, for whatever reasons, he was not able to be there.
