subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The budget vote.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I hear someone saying the budget vote. I would hesitate to accept that because there is not a minister who cannot be where he wants to be when there is a majority government. With a majority government, ministers go where they want to be. We all know that the vote on the budget the other night was not a vote of confidence in the government.
The Minister of Transport absented himself later today, as he absented himself in Halifax from a conference which had been in preparation for six months. It was pretty fundamental to Atlantic Canada. I do not know what it is like in Saskatchewan. However, for the minister at the last minute to excuse himself from a conference in Atlantic Canada that had been set up for months was a sad reflection of his concern for transportation problems in Atlantic Canada. There was great concern in Halifax when the minister did not show up. It is the same type of disappointment, but to a lesser degree, that the minister is not here today. There may be a legitimate reason for that.
Rarely in Atlantic Canada has there been such concern about where we are going in transportation. That is primarily because of the rehash of some of these new or old ideas that the minister has been talking about. I am going to come to that.
The minister says we have to be realistic with regard to transportation. There is not a member of this House who does not appreciate there has to be some realism. However, I suggest to the minister that if there were realism and only realism in transportation, this country called Canada would never have been built.
This type of narrow minded professorial, restricted theory, with no inspiration or imagination in a field that is crying for inspiration, imagination, and new energy, is one reason we have these problems in transportation. In his speech the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley) said you cannot have it both ways. Why should the people of Canada have faith in the Minister of Transport when he says we have to be realistic in our policy, and no longer have band-aids or political expediency in the area of transportation?
Never was the question of transportation more abused in more crass political ways than by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the time of the last election in his politically dishonest attempt to stay in power. Now the Minister of Transport, cloaking himself in the sackcloth of some vestal virgin, wants us to walk with him hand in hand down this little road, ride on the bumpy railbeds, and fly in the planes of this land. He wants us to do all these things and place our confidence in him and not talk about band-aids and political expediency, when the reality is that the government for 43 of the last 50 years has had responsibility for transport. It has had the chance to build rail beds, it has had the chance to take politics out of transportation and get down to basics. That is why we are a little skepti-

June 11, 1976
Transportation Policy
cal when the minister says everything will be peaches and cream and that the word politics will be taken out.
As far as some of his plans are concerned, the Minister of Transport was the minister responsible for the Wheat Board.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: He still is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is unfortunate for the Wheat Board. It was the present Minister of Transport who conceived the LIFT project-lower inventories for tomorrow. And we all know it became lower incomes for tomorrow.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It did not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
It did, because it took hundreds of thousands of acres out of production just at a time when wheat was going from about $1.05 a bushel to $4 or $5 a bushel. The farmers of Western Canada were short-changed by this classroom concept which was promulgated by the Minister of Transport. Because he sometimes wears the cloth of a politician, he sold the idea to the government, and the wheat farmers of the West were the people who lost out. We are afraid we shall lose out as a result of some of the transportation policies envisaged today.
I wish to move on now in a non-partisan way; some of the words I intend to quote were spoken by people who wear Liberal sackcloth from time to time-provincial premiers who are concerned about where the federal government is going in the field of transport and so on. I might point out that the premiers of Atlantic Canada are, one might say, bipartisan-there were two Liberal premiers and two Conservatives. But on the Maritime Council, to which I shall soon refer, there are only three- two Liberals and one Conservative. I would draw the attention of the House to the final communique of the Council of Maritime Premiers issued in Charlottetown on May 26 of this year. With regard to transportation the premiers say;
Bona fide consultation is required between governments to ensure that transportation is used to help rather than hinder economic development.
The premiers also expressed concern that the federal government is increasing cost recovery within some transportation systems without considering the effects on the over-all economy. The communique went on:
Undue reliance upon the user pay concept should be replaced by the vigorous pursuit of cost-effective solutions ...
That expresses the generality in terms of national transportation policy. Coming to specifics, one of them was mentioned by my hon. friend from Carleton-Charlotte who spoke of Bill C-61. I will read two paragraphs because they are so interesting. The one I intend to read first deals with the budget and explains why there is concern in Atlantic Canada about where transportation policy is heading.
It is, of course, easy for us all to say we are in favour of restraint, but there is real cause for concern when expenditure in an area which is so vital to Atlantic Canada, the area of transportation, is cut by over 50 per cent. Need I point out once again that we are talking here about a region of economic disparity, a region where wage levels

generally are lower than they are in the rest of the country, a region which does not enjoy the same extended economic base as other parts of Canada? Those are not just my sentiments. Those words paraphrase the feelings of the Atlantic premiers, as is clear from this later statement in the communique;
The premiers expressed disappointment in the federal budgetary restraint program as it applies to transportation expenditure. Recognizing the need for effective measures to control inflation and restore economic stability they endorse the principle of a restraint program but took issue with the discriminatory nature of the transportation section of the announced program, noting that of a total reduction of $41.2 million for the whole of Canada $21.9 or 63 per cent would affect the maritime region transportation program exclusively.
The communique went on to say;
In view of the present economic situation in the Atlantic provinces and the effect transportation has upon it, the announced transport expenditure reduction would seem to be inconsistent with programs designed to correct regional disparity.
Those words, Mr. Speaker, say it all in a nutshell. I fail to understand how someone could hope to establish a viable program of regional development, while on the other hand making such savage cuts in transportation subsidies affecting the very region which one is supposedly trying to help. It is contradictory. It is one of the reasons why the program of regional economic development has failed to produce the economic results for which members on both sides had hoped when the department was set up several years ago. It is impossible to pursue a viable program of economic development unless it is complemented and supplemented by satisfactory transportation policies. Over half of the restraint measures announced in the federal budget hit Atlantic Canada right on the nose.
Bill C-61 was mentioned by other speakers and I shall not spend too much time on that aspect. As for Bill C-87, fortunately the government House leader has agreed to take another look at it. Some people say it will put an end to exports of grain and flour. These are things which give rise to legitimate concern among people in the region regardless of their political stripe.
I mentioned earlier the comments made by the Council of Maritime Premiers on budgetary restraints which feels, quite rightly, that a cut of over 50 per cent is a little heavy for an area of this kind which cannot stand that kind of cut.
They had this to say about the coasting trade in reference to Bill C-61:
The Premiers expressed concern that the safeguards required to protect regional industries against high transportation costs which would result from the removal of Commonwealth shipping in the coasting trade do not appear to have been adequately provided in either the new act or proposed regulations. The Premiers said that at a meeting of the Council of Maritime Premiers and the Premier of Newfoundland with the Honourable Jean Marchand in September, 1973, it was announced that Canada would withdraw from the British Commonwealth Shipping Agreement and reserve coastal shipping to Canadian flag vessels. At the same time, assurance was given by the federal minister that safeguards would be introduced to protect regional industries against high transportation costs.
The Premiers today are sending a telegram to the Honourable Otto Lang urging him to permit the use of non-Canadian vessels according to the dictates of availability and cost. This is essential to enable
June 11, 1976

maritime industries to benefit from one of the region's natural advantages.
I should also like to refer to the telex of May 26 signed by the chairman of the Council of Maritime Premiers, Premier A. B. Campbell of P.E.I. He is a concerned premier of Atlantic Canada and he had this to say in his telegram:
Further to our telex to you of December 16, 1975, and other representations made to you and your predecessor, we are still deeply concerned about Bill C-61. Recent representations from industry have heightened this concern, giving it a new dimension.
In view of this, we now urge you to take action which will retain for Atlantic industries their access to non-Canadian vessels for the coasting trade without serious impediment in the form of the necessity for either expensive or difficult-to-obtain waivers, licences or permits. Availability of suitable vessels and their cost should be the criteria for the selection of carriers, with the decision resting with the shipper.
Existing industry and future industrial development in the Atlantic provinces will be seriously affected if this bill, and those regulations of which we have been made aware to date, come into effect. This legislation would tend to transform the Atlantic provinces into inland provinces in so far as coastal shipping is concerned without their concomitant advantages. High transportation cost to and from markets is already one of the most serious obstacles restricting growth in this region. By restricting competition, Bill C-61 will increase these costs for water, rail or truck.
We urge you to withdraw or change this legislation as it pertains to coastal shipping and to permit the use of non-Canadian vessels according to the dictates of availability and cost, thereby enabling our industries to benefit from one of this region's natural advantages.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the remarks that have been made today are those not of partisan, political creatures that are worried about band-aids, but of Canadians worried about fundamentals. We want to know how this new policy of user pay as it applies to mature and immature regions of Canada is going to work. Perhaps the definition of mature is that we should remove subsidies or make cutbacks, for some paradoxical reason, in Atlantic Canada, which everyone would admit is an area of economic disability, that this in the minister's eyes will be considered a mature region. He did not say anything about that today. We have all heard about western alienation, Quebec separation, and B.C. isolation. I say that we are going to cry out for our maritime rights unless we get a better deal from the Minister of Transport.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-TRANSPORTATION-"USER PAY" CONCEPT AS DEFINED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale) would like to take part in this debate before the day ends, so I assure him that my remarks will be very brief and will leave him plenty of time, provided that Mr. Speaker calls on him when I sit down.
I should like to join with others in commending the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) for putting down this subject for debate on this opposition day. Like many days in this House of Commons, it is not a day on which we make decisions or arrive at any conclusions, but I do think it has been one of the better days of debate on transportation policy. Arguments have been presented from both sides, there has been a good deal of philosophy and many suggestions, and I hope that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and his department will take cognizance of what has been said in this day's debate.
It will come as no surprise to anyone in this House when I say that the reason that I ask for the floor for a few minutes is to underline once more what I think is one of
Transportation Policy
the requirements of a transportation industry that serves the best interests of the country. That requirement is good employer-employee relations.
I come now to what might be called my favourite subject. I think that one of the ways to establish and to maintain good employer-employee relations is to have good pension programs. It has been a long struggle to get the pension programs of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific to their present level, but there is a tremendous need for still further improvement.
The fact is that nearly two years ago, as a result of one of the distputes in the railway industry, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) appointed Dr. Noel Hall as a special commissioner to examine all aspects of railway pensions. When I say all aspects, I refer to all railways in Canada, to the pensions of those already retired, the pension plans of those still working, and so on. We do not yet have this report. The Minister of Labour has promised it "soon" so often that the meaning of the word is hard to grasp, but I do hope we will get it within a few weeks. The difficulty is that it is taking so long to get the report and that many pensioners who had hoped to benefit from it have died, and others wonder whether they will live long enough to see the benefits of this study.
I have two things I want to say. First, I urge the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour, when they do get Dr. Noel Hall's report, to study it very carefully and if, as I am sure there will be, there are in it recommendations that will improve the pension position of railway workers I hope they will do all they can to see to it that those recommendations are implemented without delay.
The other thing I want to say is simply by way of underlining the point that I made in a question which I put to the Minister of Transport this morning. Although we have been waiting for the Noel Hall report a long time, one can at least say that the Canadian National Railways a short while ago did put into effect an increase, a small one but nevertheless an increase, in the pensions of those already retired or their survivors. It seems to me that that action by the Canadian National Railways should be matched by the Canadian Pacific. The point of my question to the Minister of Transport was to urge that he have a serious talk with CPR about this matter. I appreciated his reply that he would do so, and I simply rise now to make it part of the record at the end as well as at the beginning of this day. I hope this is something the minister will do at the earliest possible opportunity.
I agree with all who have spoken in this House as to the importance of transportation to this country and as to the need for making improvements. But I repeat that we will have a healthy transportation policy if we have happy and satisfied employees, and one of the best ways to achieve good employer-employee relations is to establish and maintain the best possible pension plan. Real improvements have to be made for our railway workers, and they must be made soon.

Mr. Speaker, I was moved to make a few remarks in this debate by the response of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) today which made us more clearly aware of the direction we

I really feel the minister did a remarkable job in describing for us in rather simple terms exactly the direction we are taking. I cannot accept the suggestion we heard a few minutes ago, and earlier today from the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), that in fact the result of the minister's remarks today was greater confusion. The minister's response seemed to me to be a remarkable clarification of the issue, and I thank him for it.
Having regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Abbott), and particularly those regarding the airline industry and its response to the cost factors and arguments put forward by the minister, I feel perhaps some response should be made, particularly in respect of general aviation in this country.
The aviation industry has obviously been a resource assistance to opening up this country. This must be recognized by the minister and his officials who contemplate this idea of cost effect and the user pay concept in the total transportation field. If in fact the airline industry is to be consulted with respect to how airports will be built in the future and what facilities are needed for the movement of passengers, and in respect of runways required for future type aircraft, and those sorts of things, then it seems to me these facilities will also be used by aircraft that do not require luxurious buildings, 10,000-foot runways, and six feet of concrete at the threshold. In fact these facilities will be used by aircraft flying into our hinterlands and carrying small packages on an express basis between cities. In this way we will have facilities substantially over-built for the type of aircraft using them.
I trust and I believe, because of what the minister indicated today, that there is a conscious awareness of this fact when considering the user pay concept. I trust there is to be some realization that a great deal of the time the use to be made of these facilities which are substantially overbuilt will be by these small aircraft, and that as a consequence some reasonable approach will be made in respect of that reality.
I should like to make one further suggestion, and I commend this to the minister's attention, in respect of the movement of passengers by rail and by other means. The minister indicated he really thought it would be unreasonable for anyone to suggest that people should not be moved by bus along an unused railway line. I hope he has in mind the fact that some people may not be travelling now by bus as a matter of preference over rail travel, but rather because of the mode of transportation that is available, the type of facility, etc. Many of them are using this mode of transportation because of the misuse and disrepair of the available mode of transportation.
We have to be careful that we do not impose on the people our position of preference in respect of transportation. We must pay more attention to the fact that people may not rather move by train than by bus, or by bus than by train. Having in mind some of the bus service between Toronto and Windsor and the length of time it takes, I feel certain that most of my constituents would express a preference for rail travel over bus, even if we were able to improve that service.

One must also remember the Bruce-Grey Peninsula where in fact there used to be train passenger service available. That service no longer exists. One would hope that in fact we would not place ourselves in the position in respect of such areas that we will only be looking at the possibility of a bus service as opposed to the reinstitution of train service.
May I also say in respect of the situation in that part of my riding of Peeley Island that the transportation services seem to be deteriorating. There are pockets of people who will never be able to support the type of transportation they need. It would be unreasonable to suggest that the 200 island people should pay the total cost of an air or boat service to that island.
Let me indicate again that after listening to the minister today I feel confident that, notwithstanding the user pay concept, there will be an improvement in over-all transportation policy. I feel that in fact there must be a substantial amount of reasoning behind that concept to be followed by cost effectiveness, with the realization there is still the principle that the taxpayers as a whole must bear some of the costs of transportation. Having pointed out some of the concerns I have, and having expressed my complete satisfaction with the general principle as outlined by the minister, I want to compliment the minister again for a straightforward and clear exposing of this issue today.

Let me refer to the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). When he began to speak I thought he was going to get at the heart of the problem, namely, top priority items in implementing a workable transportation policy for this country. He then moved from what I thought was the key issue. He limited his remarks concerning the employees strictly to pensions. Pensions represent an important part of the benefit package of our working force, and I agree with the concern expressed by the hon. member for that segment of the working force involved in transportation.
I stress, however, that there is no point in spending hundreds of millions of dollars on improving transportation in Canada unless we have full and open co-operation from members of the work force who are involved in that aspect of Canadian life. There are thousands and thousands of lost man years of effort in our transportation system due to strikes. If the transportation policy which has been submitted to the thirtieth parliament by the government is going to work, we must first involve the nation's work force in the planning and implementation of this policy. There is no sense in improving the arteries to the port of Vancouver and in building more grain elevators so we can service the world faster and better, if the people manning and operating the system do not have the right attitude toward it.
A fundamental priority in making the new transportation policy of the government work-and I am basically sympathetic to it and I have worked pretty hard to gain an understanding of it-would, in my opinion, be the involvement of the employees and work force of this nation. We can no longer continue to serve this country well and to take our part and place in the world with a labour management philosophy which involves confrontation. We will have to turn to Europe and look at the results of co-determination, look at the results of industrial democratization of other industrial countries and integrate them into our lives in Canada as a first priority to keep us from spinning our wheels in trying to update our great transportation machine in Canada.
For example, I look at such things as the STOL experiment. I can understand $25 million or $30 million being thrown away on an experiment, but I cannot understand STOL when the need is for a high speed railway down the dense corridor of Canada. I notice that my good friend, the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley), was commenting on the St. Lawrence Seaway and pointing out that the administration burden has decreased. That is probably the only example we could find in government agencies where it has. But I should like to put it into perspective. Here we have a $6 million administrative burden for $23 million of revenue which cost $22 million in direct costs and requires a $42 million subsidy from the people of Canada. If that is "user pay", then something has to give.
We in other parts of Canada-and I am very fortunate in coming from the port of Vancouver-have had an excellent track record in having been able to pay for our own facilities. We produce over 54 per cent of the profits earned
Transportation Policy
by the National Habours Board of Canada. We would like to see the port of Vancouver developed and utilized. The port of Vancouver is not just in Bnrrard Inlet or on the Pacific coast, or on the tidemark line. The port of Vancouver starts somewhere up in the hinterland, and I am speaking specifically of the mechanics of the port. If we resolve the problems of that port and utilize it to its full effectiveness, we will have to start organizing the dispatch and utilization of all modes of transport and co-ordinate them. I have had more input from union members out there than I have had from management in the utilization of facilities that already exist there. If we dispatch trains from Kamloops and take away the competitive forces between the grain elevators there, we could increase our ship loadings. We cannot increase our ship loadings unless we have the input and co-operation of the labour force.
Time is running out on me, Mr. Speaker, but there are two more things I would like to say. We are talking about the user pay concept in transport. This means that we will have to start decentralizing the decision-making process because we in the west are just about at the end of our tether about some of the decisions imposed on us by the mandarins, bureaucrats, and so called experts here in Ottawa.
When we were out travelling on the west coast with the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications we visited the port of Seattle and the airport owned by the port. That airport is one of the finest installations that anyone interested in transport could visit. It has satellite stations, and the main terminal is served by a computerized underground railroad. It has fantastic immigration facilities so that people emerging from large airlines do not have to wait for hours. The customs and parking facilities are also excellent. Everything is made for man, as it should be. That airport cost only $150 million. It has two runways. It is financed locally, the interest is paid, it is non-profit and self-liquidating. Then I look at the over building for which we have a tendency here in Canada, and at the $450 million minimum that Mirabel will cost us. There is something wrong with us in Canada. We are a country of 24 million people and we cannot afford this kind of luxury, this nonsense, this over building in the light of examples of other airports on this continent.
The other thing we do in air transportation is to base everything on seasonal demands. We place full page advertising for charter flights to Europe on our national airline. We advertise holidays here and there, we tell people to spend their dollars somewhere else. The demand on our airports is to take care of the peak summer tourist season. Is this the user pay concept? The guy who has to travel back and forth selling and buying goods and seeking orders has to pay the load for the whole. We have to put this into perspective. The regular user of our airline and transportation systems is prepared to pay and wants to pay, but why should we pay for facilities that are over built and over designed for 60 days of the year for the tourist industry? This should be rationally considered in our consideration of the user pay principle.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AID FOR MAIN A DIEU, NOVA SCOTIA

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AID FOR MAIN A DIEU, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as many hon. members know, a disaster recently took place in a community in Nova Scotia called Main a Dieu which suffered from a very severe fire which has caused great damage to the community and the surrounding area.
Among the many unhappy consequences it is obvious that there will be severe unemployment, although I hope it will be temporary. In the face of this, and along the lines of our response last year to the Springhill community disaster, we are going to make available immediately some funds from the Local Initiatives Program to try to provide the necessary resources for clean-up, rehabilitation, and employment. The amount has not yet been determined. That is simply because I have just been apprised of this,

and we have not yet had the opportunity to determine exactly how much will be required. However, that will be settled in a matter of a very few days.
Applications for projects designed to aid the community and employ local people will be considered as soon as they are received. All projects submitted under this special phase of the Local Initiatives Program should be capable of immediate implementation, and they will be allowed to begin just as soon as they can be put into operation.
Project officers will be available to work with local organizations and the citizens of Main a Dieu and to assist them in designing projects. As I say, this is being provided to the community of Main a Dieu in view of the very unusual circumstances involved, and although the Local Initiatives Program is primarily intended to relieve seasonal unemployment, it is also designed to aid and improve local communities. I think these circumstances really do fit, and I hope this will receive the approval of hon. members.
